Ramsey’s Witnesses

Mauro Di Nasso ††thanks: email: mauro.di.nasso@unipi.it Affiliation: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Pisa, Largo Bruno Pontecorvo 5, 56127 Pisa, Italy     Lorenzo Luperi Baglini ††thanks: email: lorenzo.luperi@unimi.it Affiliation: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Milano, Via Saldini 50, 20133 Milano, Italy     Marcello Mamino ††thanks: email: marcello.mamino@unipi.it Affiliation: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Pisa, Largo Bruno Pontecorvo 5, 56127 Pisa, Italy     Rosario Mennuni ††thanks: email: R.Mennuni@posteo.net     Mariaclara Ragosta ††thanks: email: mariaclara@kam.mff.cuni.cz Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics (KAM), Charles University, Malostranské náměstí 25, Praha 1, Czech Republic
Abstract

We introduce the notion of Ramsey partition regularity, a generalisation of partition regularity involving infinitary configurations. We provide characterisations of this notion in terms of certain ultrafilters related to tensor products and dubbed Ramsey’s witnesses; and we also consider their nonstandard counterparts as pairs of hypernatural numbers, called Ramsey pairs. These characterisations are then used to determine whether various configurations involving polynomials and exponentials are Ramsey partition regular over the natural numbers. In particular, this provides negative answers to several questions recently posed by Kra, Moreira, Richter and Robertson.

1 Introduction

Since the 1970s, applications of ultrafilters to combinatorics have been widely studied, producing a wealth of results, especially in the area of Ramsey theory; see the comprehensive monograph [HS11]. In recent years, the close connection between the space of ultrafilters β​ℕ\beta\mathbb{N} and nonstandard extensions ∗ℕ{}^{*}\mathbb{N} of the natural numbers has been thoroughly investigated, providing an alternative approach that has revealed useful for formalising Ramsey properties in a simple and manageable way, and that has also made it possible to prove some new results in the area of arithmetic Ramsey theory.

The latter is a branch of combinatorics concerned with the “abundance” of certain arithmetic patterns in the natural numbers. A typical problem in this area is to determine whether a given configuration is ubiquitous enough that one is forced to find instances of it in some piece of every finite partition of ℕ\mathbb{N}.

In this area, it is customary to call partitions colourings. For instance, a classical theorem by I. Schur [Sch16] states that, whenever the natural numbers are coloured with finitely many colours, say ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}={C}_{1}\cup\ldots\cup{C}_{r}, then one of the CiC_{i} contains a triple of distinct elements a,b,ca,b,c such that a+b=ca+b=c. Such a triple is called a monochromatic solution of the equation x+y=zx+y=z, and the existence of monochromatic solutions in all colourings is the statement that the aforementioned equation is partition regular.

It is natural to ask which other equations have the same property. Albeit the linear case is well-understood by a classical result of R. Rado [Rad33], the polynomial one is still very far from being settled; for instance, whether the Pythagorean equation x2+y2=z2x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2} is partition regular is still unknown, and one of the long-standing open problems in the area.

The notion of partition regularity is not limited to solutions to Diophantine equations. In general, a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of subsets of a set XX is partition regular (PR) over XX if it is closed under taking supersets and, for all finite colourings X=C1∪…∪CrX=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} there exists i≤ri\leq r such that Ci∈ℱC_{i}\in\mathcal{F}; and it is strongly partition regular (SPR) over XX if, furthermore, for all Y∈ℱY\in\mathcal{F} the family ℱ∩𝒫⁡(Y)\mathcal{F}\cap\mathcal{P}(Y) is PR over YY, i.e. if for all finite colourings Y=C1∪…∪CrY=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} there exists i≤ri\leq r such that Ci∈ℱC_{i}\in\mathcal{F}.

If PP is some property that can be satisfied by a set, with a small abuse we will say that the property PP is PR if the family ℱP≔{A⊆X∣P​ is true for ​A}\mathcal{F}_{P}\coloneqq\{A\subseteq X\mid P\text{ is true for }A\} is PR. So, for example, Schur’s Theorem says that the property of containing some x,y,zx,y,z with x+y=zx+y=z is partition regular. Another celebrated example is van der Waerden’s Theorem [va27], establishing strong partition regularity for containing arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

Problems in arithmetic Ramsey theory have been tackled by employing a variety of methods; as mentioned above, one that attracted significant attention in recent years is to exploit the strict connection between spaces of ultrafilters and their algebra and nonstandard extensions of ℕ\mathbb{N}. We now briefly recall what this amounts to; see e.g. [DN15, LB19, DNGL19] for a more detailed treatment.

The link between partition regularity of a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of subsets of XX and ultrafilters on XX stems from the well-known facts that

  1. 1.

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is PR over XX if and only if there exists an ultrafilter uu over XX such that u⊆ℱu\subseteq\mathcal{F}; such a uu is called a witness of the partition regularity of ℱ\mathcal{F}; and

  2. 2.

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is SPR over XX if and only if ℱ≠∅\mathcal{F}\neq\emptyset and for all Y∈ℱY\in\mathcal{F} there is a witness u⊆ℱu\subseteq\mathcal{F} containing YY.

As for nonstandard extensions of ℕ\mathbb{N}, recall that these are elementary extensions of the natural numbers, that is, larger structures satisfying the transfer principle for first-order formulas.11 1 Here ℕ\mathbb{N} is equipped with its full first-order structure, that is, with relation symbols for every subset of each of its Cartesian powers. For example, this means that, for every subset A⊆ℕkA\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{k}, there is an associated nonstandard extension ∗A⊆∗ℕk{}^{\ast}A\subseteq{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{k} that satisfies the same first-order properties as AA: e.g., if AA is the set of even natural numbers, then ∗A{}^{\ast}A is precisely the set of those elements of ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} of the form 2​α2\alpha, for a suitable α∈∗ℕ\alpha\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}. Sets of the form ∗A{}^{\ast}A, and more generally internal subsets of ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}, are well-behaved in a number of senses. Crucially, they satisfy the same elementary properties as subsets of ℕ\mathbb{N}, e.g. every nonempty internal subset has a least element. Furthermore, they obey the overspill principle: whenever an internal set contains arbitrarily large natural numbers, then it must also contain an element larger than ℕ\mathbb{N}; so, for instance, ℕ\mathbb{N} is not internal.

Elements of some nonstandard extension ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} are called hypernatural numbers, and they and their tuples bear a natural relation to ultrafilters on ℕ\mathbb{N} and its Cartesian powers. Namely, for (α1,…,αk)∈ℕk∗\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}^{k}, the set22 2 Other notations common in the literature are u(α1,…,αk)u_{\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)} and tp⁡(α1,…,αk)\operatorname{tp}(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}).

𝔲(α1,…,αk)≔{A⊆ℕk∣(α1,…,αk)∈A∗}\tp\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)\coloneqq\{A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{k}\mid\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)\in{}^{\ast}{A}\}

belongs to β​ℕk\beta\mathbb{N}^{k}—that is, it is an ultrafilter on ℕk\mathbb{N}^{k}. Conversely, every u∈β​ℕku\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{k} is of the form u=𝔲⁡(α1,…,αk)u=\tp\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right) for a suitable (α1,…,αk)∈ℕk∗\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}^{k}}, provided ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} is 𝔠+\mathfrak{c}^{+}-saturated.

Throughout the paper, we work in such a ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}. We write (α1,…,αk)∼(β1,…,βk)\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)\sim\left(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{k}\right), and say that these tuples are equivalent, whenever 𝔲⁡(α1,…,αk)=𝔲⁡(β1,…,βk)\tp\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\right)=\tp\left(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{k}\right). The equivalence classes of this relation correspond, as explained above, to ultrafilters u∈β​ℕku\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{k}. For each such uu, the associated ∼\sim-equivalence class called the monad of uu, and its elements generators of uu. It is well-known that combinatorial properties of uu can be rephrased in terms of properties of its monad. For finitary configurations, that is, properties expressible by a first-order formula, this can be done by using the following fundamental property. See e.g. [DNGL19, Proposition 9.1], or [LB19, Theorem 5.4] for a more general version.

Fact 1.1.

A formula φ⁡(x1,…,xn)\varphi({x}_{1},\ldots,{x}_{n}) is PR, that is, for every finite colouring ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}={C}_{1}\cup\ldots\cup{C}_{r} there is a monochromatic (a1,…,an)({a}_{1},\ldots,{a}_{n}) such that ℕ⊧φ⁡(a1,…,an)\mathbb{N}\models\varphi({a}_{1},\ldots,{a}_{n}), if and only if there are α1∼…∼αn{\alpha}_{1}\sim\ldots\sim{\alpha}_{n} such that ℕ∗⊧φ(α1,…,αn){}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}\models\varphi({\alpha}_{1},\ldots,{\alpha}_{n}).

Above, ℕ∗⊧φ(α1,…,αn){}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}\models\varphi({\alpha}_{1},\ldots,{\alpha}_{n}) means that the formula φ⁡(α1,…,αn)\varphi({\alpha}_{1},\ldots,{\alpha}_{n}) holds in ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}. Combining this with the ultrafilter characterisation of partition regularity we see that, for instance, Schur’s Theorem is, in this language, the statement that there are α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma in ∗ℕ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} such that ∗ℕ⊧α+β=γ{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}\models\alpha+\beta=\gamma.

Over the years Schur’s result has been strengthened in various directions. Most notably, in [Hin74] N. Hindman proved the following infinitary extension:

Theorem (Hindman’s Theorem).

For every finite colouring of ℕ\mathbb{N} there exists an infinite increasing sequence (xi)i∈ℕ(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} such that the set of all finite sums FS((xi)i∈ℕ)={xi1+…+xik∣k∈ℕ,i1<…<ik}\text{FS}((x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}})=\{x_{i_{1}}+\ldots+x_{i_{k}}\mid k\in\mathbb{N},i_{1}<\ldots<i_{k}\} is monochromatic.

Theorem (Hindman’s Theorem). is the prototype of the results on the existence of infinite monochromatic configurations, which can be seen as leaps from the realm of finite mathematics to the world of infinite combinatorics.

Typically these statements are closely related, in one way or another, to Ramsey’s Theorem [Ram30]. Let us recall the 22-dimensional case of the latter which, when applied to X=ℕX=\mathbb{N}, is the case that we will study in the rest of the paper. Write [X]2≔{{x1,x2}∣x1,x2∈X,x1≠x2}[X]^{2}\coloneqq\{\{x_{1},x_{2}\}\mid x_{1},x_{2}\in X,x_{1}\neq x_{2}\}.

Theorem (Ramsey’s Theorem for pairs).

Let XX be an infinite set. For all finite partitions [X]2=C1∪…∪Cr[X]^{2}=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} there exist i≤ri\leq r and an infinite H⊆XH\subseteq X such that [H]2⊆Ci[H]^{2}\subseteq C_{i}.

For convenience, when X=ℕX=\mathbb{N}, we identify [H]2[H]^{2} with {(h1,h2)∈H2∣h1<h2}\{(h_{1},h_{2})\in H^{2}\mid h_{1}<h_{2}\}.

A direct application of Theorem (Ramsey’s Theorem for pairs). shows that the family ℱ\mathcal{F} of those A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N} such that there is an infinite HH with {h1+h2∣(h1,h2)∈[H]2}⊆A\{h_{1}+h_{2}\mid(h_{1},h_{2})\in[H]^{2}\}\subseteq A is SPR. The analogous statement also holds if sums are replaced by products but, notably, sums and products cannot be combined. Indeed, a theorem proved by N. Hindman in [Hin84, Theorem 2.11], another proof of which recently appeared in [HIL23, Theorem 3.1], states the following.

Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the family of those A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N} such that

∃H⊆ℕH is infinite and ∀(x,y)∈[H]2(x+y,x⋅y∈A).\exists H\subseteq\mathbb{N}\ H\text{ is infinite and }\forall(x,y)\in[H]^{2}\;(x+y,x\cdot y\in A).

Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is not PR.

This is (a failure of) the kind of “Ramsey partition regularity” statements (see Definition 3.6) that we study in this paper, namely: for which formulas φ⁡(x,y,z1,…,zn)\varphi\left(x,y,z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right), given a finite colouring of ℕ\mathbb{N}, one can find an infinite set HH such that for all (x,y)∈[H]2(x,y)\in[H]^{2} there exist monochromatic z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n} such that φ⁡(x,y,z1,…,zn)\varphi\left(x,y,z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right) holds? E.g., in the theorem above, φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) is the formula (x≠y)∧(x+y=z)∧(x⋅y=t)(x\neq y)\wedge(x+y=z)\wedge(x\cdot y=t).

Because of the infinitary nature of these statements, Fact 1.1 does not directly apply. Nevertheless, one may still study such problems via nonstandard methods by employing the following definition, not to be confused with that of “Ramsey ultrafilters” (also known as “selective ultrafilters”).

Definition 1.2.

We call an ultrafilter u∈β​ℕ2u\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{2} a Ramsey’s witness (RW) if for all A∈uA\in u there exists an infinite H⊆ℕH\subseteq\mathbb{N} such that [H]2⊆A[H]^{2}\subseteq A. We also write RW\mathrm{RW} for the subset of β​ℕ2\beta\mathbb{N}^{2} consisting of all uu as above, and say that (α,β)∈ℕ2∗(\alpha,\beta)\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}^{2} is a Ramsey pair, if 𝔲⁡(α,β)∈RW\tp(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathrm{RW}. In this case, we write (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}.

By Theorem (Ramsey’s Theorem for pairs)., the family of all A⊆ℕ2A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2} such that there exists an infinite H⊆ℕH\subseteq\mathbb{N} with [H]2⊆A[H]^{2}\subseteq A is SPR. Equivalently, every such AA is contained in some u∈RWu\in\mathrm{RW}; equivalently, ∗A{}^{\ast}A contains a Ramsey pair.

Theorem 3.8 is our main technical result. It provides a “Ramsey” version of Fact 1.1, that is, a characterisation of Ramsey partition regularity statements in terms of properties of Ramsey pairs. From this characterisation we deduce several results in the style of the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem).. Let us state some of them in the language we just introduced.

Theorem A.

If (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a Ramsey pair, then

  1. 1.

    α+β≁α⋅β\alpha+\beta\nsim\alpha\cdot\beta (Theorem 4.1),

  2. 2.

    α⋅β≁αβ\alpha\cdot\beta\nsim\alpha^{\beta} (Example 5.24),

  3. 3.

    αβ≁βα\alpha^{\beta}\nsim\beta^{\alpha} (Example 5.23), and

  4. 4.

    f⁡(α)⋅2β≁g⁡(α,β)f(\alpha)\cdot 2^{\beta}\nsim g(\alpha,\beta), where f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and g∈ℤ⁡[x,y]g\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] (special case of Example 5.26).

Point 1 is a restatement of the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem)., of which we provide a short nonstandard proof. It is known [Sah18, Theorem 2] that every finite colouring of the naturals contains a monochromatic quadruple a,b,a⋅b,aba,b,a\cdot b,a^{b}. Point 2 says that the Ramsey version of this does not hold, not even for a⋅b,aba\cdot b,a^{b}, i.e., there is a finite colouring of ℕ\mathbb{N} such that no increasing sequence (ai)i∈ℕ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} is such that the set {ai⋅aj∣i<j}∪{aiaj∣i<j}\{a_{i}\cdot a_{j}\mid i<j\}\cup\{a_{i}^{a_{j}}\mid i<j\} is monochromatic. See also [DNR24, DNR22] for partition regularity of exponential configurations. Points 3 and 4 correspond to similar Ramsey properties.

We also study the Ramsey partition regularity of polynomial equations. Namely, given a nonzero polynomial P∈ℤ⁡[x1,…,xn]P\in\mathbb{Z}[{x}_{1},\ldots,{x}_{n}], we investigate whether the formula P⁡(x1,…,xn)=0P({x}_{1},\ldots,{x}_{n})=0 is Ramsey PR. In the two-variable case, there are no Ramsey PR equations (Proposition 5.2). Our next result concerns certain 33-variable polynomials.

Theorem B (5.10 and 5.11).

Let P,Q∈ℤ⁡[x]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be nonzero polynomials with P⁡(0)=Q⁡(0)=0P(0)=Q(0)=0 and a,n∈ℕa,n\in\mathbb{N}. The following are equivalent.

  1. 1.

    There are α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma with (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) a Ramsey pair such that a​αn+P⁡(β)=Q⁡(γ)a\alpha^{n}+P(\beta)=Q(\gamma);

  2. 2.

    a​xn+P⁡(y)−Q⁡(z)ax^{n}+P(y)-Q(z) is either a⁡(x+y−z)a(x+y-z) or a⁡(x−y+z)a(x-y+z).

In other words, up to multiplying everything by a constant, the only two equations of the form a​xn+P⁡(y)=Q⁡(z)ax^{n}+P(y)=Q(z) that are Ramsey PR in x,yx,y are Schur’s equation x+y=zx+y=z and the equation x−y=−zx-y=-z. An interesting property of the latter is that, contrarily to Schur’s equation, it cannot be solved by tensor pairs (Remark 5.13). Theorem B rules out the Ramsey partition regularity of plenty of equations, ranging from some whose partition regularity is open, such as the Pythagorean equation x2+y2=z2x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}, to equations of the form y−x=zny-x=z^{n}, for n≥2n\geq 2, that are known to be PR, see [BFM96, Theorem C].

Similar Ramsey partition regularity problems were posed in [KMRR25], which contains questions arising from the solution [MRR19] to Erdős’ B+CB+C conjecture, arguably the most important recent result in combinatorics. In particular, Theorem B answers in the negative several questions from Sections 3.3 and 3.4 of [KMRR25], in the stronger PR version, albeit in the form without shifts.

For instance, in the language of the present work, the shiftless PR version of [KMRR25, Question 3.15] amounts to asking whether the equation x2+y=zx^{2}+y=z is Ramsey PR. In [Ack25, Theorem 1.5] it is shown that this equation is Ramsey PR over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, and in fact that the same holds with x2x^{2} replaced by any P⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[x]P(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x] of degree at least 22. This fails over ℕ\mathbb{N} by Theorem B and, after a preprint version of this paper was circulated, E. Ackelsberg gave an explicit 55-colouring witnessing that x2+y=zx^{2}+y=z is not Ramsey PR, see [Ack25, Section 11.1]. Analogously, Theorem B answers in the negative the PR shiftless versions of [KMRR25, Questions 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.15, 3.19, 3.20], as well as the variant of [KMRR25, Question 3.16] with monomials on the left hand side but arbitrary polynomials without constant term on the right hand one.

Theorems A and B demonstrate that being Ramsey PR significantly strengthens being merely PR. One may wonder what happens to other properties classically known to be PR. In this direction, another application of our results is a proof that van der Waerden’s Theorem does not admit a “Ramsey version”, not even in the case of 33-term arithmetic progressions.

Theorem C (Proposition 5.14).

If α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma and (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a Ramsey pair, then α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma do not form, in any order, an arithmetic progression.

The paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 we will prove several properties of Ramsey pairs and characterise them in terms of tensor pairs. In Section 3, we introduce several versions of Ramsey partition regularity and characterise them in ultrafilter and nonstandard terms. In Section 4 we study these notions for the formula φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) that appears in the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem)., and give a very compact proof of the latter. In Section 5 we prove Theorems A, B and C, and in our final Section 6 we collect some open problems that we believe deserve further study.

2 Ramsey’s witnesses

In this paper, ℕ\mathbb{N} denotes the set of positive integers. We assume familiarity with the basics of nonstandard methods, for which we refer the reader to, e.g., [Gol98], but we briefly recall some well-known facts on tensor pairs.

The relationship between ultrafilters on ℕ\mathbb{N} and on ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} is intricate, as the product filter u×vu\times v of two ultrafilters on ℕ\mathbb{N}, generated by the family {A×B∣A∈u,B∈v}\{A\times B\mid A\in u,B\in v\}, is not in general an ultrafilter on ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2}. Among all the ultrafilters that extend u×vu\times v, one plays a special role in many applications, namely the tensor product u⊗vu\otimes v.

Definition 2.1.

Given u,v∈β​ℕu,v\in\beta\mathbb{N}, the tensor product u⊗vu\otimes v is the ultrafilter on ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} defined as follows: for all A⊆ℕ2A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}, we let

A∈u⊗v⇔{n∈ℕ∣{m∈ℕ∣(n,m)∈A}∈v}∈u.A\in u\otimes v\Leftrightarrow\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid\{m\in\mathbb{N}\mid(n,m)\in A\}\in v\}\in u.

Given (α,β)∈ℕ2∗(\alpha,\beta)\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{2}, we say that (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair if 𝔲⁡(α,β)\tp(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor product.

The tensor product can also be considered in arbitrary dimensions and is associative, hence it makes sense to talk of tensor triples, tensor kk-uples, etc. However, in this paper we will mostly work with tensor products in dimension 2. Note that, almost by definition, if (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair then 𝔲⁡(α,β)=𝔲⁡(α)⊗𝔲⁡(β)\tp(\alpha,\beta)=\tp(\alpha)\otimes\tp(\beta). For a detailed study of tensor products we refer to [LB19]. In more model-theoretic language, (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair if the type of α\alpha over ℕ∪{β}\mathbb{N}\cup\{\beta\} is a coheir of its restriction to ℕ\mathbb{N}, that is, is finitely satisfiable in ℕ\mathbb{N}, which amounts to the following.

Fact 2.2.

The pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is tensor if and only if for every A∈𝔲⁡(α,β)A\in\tp(\alpha,\beta) there is n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that A∈𝔲⁡(n,β)A\in\tp(n,\beta).

This point of view is exploited for example in [CZ22].

Combinatorial applications of tensor pairs by means of nonstandard methods are based on their characterisation given by C. Puritz in [Pur72, Theorem 3.4] (for higher dimensions, see [LB19, Theorem 4.22]33 3 In the cited result, there is a missing assumption that α1,…,αn{\alpha}_{1},\ldots,{\alpha}_{n} are not standard.). Before recalling Puritz’ Theorem, let us review some prerequisites. See e.g. [DN14, DN15, DNGL19, LB19] for further details.

Notation 2.3.

Throughout the paper we treat functions f:ℕk→ℕf:\mathbb{N}^{k}\to\mathbb{N} as symbols in the language of the full structure on ℕ\mathbb{N}; in practice this means that, if α∈∗ℕk\alpha\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{k}, its image under the nonstandard extension of ff to ∗ℕk{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{k} will be denoted by f⁡(α)f(\alpha) instead of f∗(α){}^{\ast}f(\alpha). Similarly, we use the symbol ff also for the induced map β​ℕk→β​ℕ\beta\mathbb{N}^{k}\to\beta\mathbb{N} (which is well-defined by Fact 2.4 below). We write ℕ(α)\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha) for the definable closure of α\alpha, namely

ℕ(α)≔{f(α)∣f:ℕ→ℕ}.\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha)\coloneqq\{f(\alpha)\mid f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\}.
Fact 2.4.

Let α∈∗ℕn\alpha\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{n}, β∈∗ℕm\beta\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{m}, f:ℕn→ℕlf:\mathbb{N}^{n}\to\mathbb{N}^{l}, and g:ℕm→ℕlg:\mathbb{N}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{l}.

  1. 1.

    If α∼β\alpha\sim\beta then f⁡(α)∼f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\sim f(\beta).

  2. 2.

    If f⁡(α)∼αf(\alpha)\sim\alpha then f⁡(α)=αf(\alpha)=\alpha.

  3. 3.

    The following are equivalent.

    1. (a)

      f⁡(α)∼g⁡(β)f(\alpha)\sim g(\beta).

    2. (b)

      There exists β′∼β\beta^{\prime}\sim\beta such that f⁡(α)=g⁡(β′)f(\alpha)=g(\beta^{\prime}).

  4. 4.

    If α,β∈∗ℕ\alpha,\beta\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}, α∼β\alpha\sim\beta, and α<β\alpha<\beta, then β−α\beta-\alpha is infinite.

Fact 2.5 (Puritz).

Let (α,β)∈ℕ2∗(\alpha,\beta)\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}^{2}}. Then (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair if and only if for all f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} we have f⁡(β)∈ℕf(\beta)\in\mathbb{N} or α<f⁡(β)\alpha<f(\beta).

The following remarks are well-known, and can be easily proven by using Fact 2.5.

Remark 2.6.

If (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair and β∉ℕ\beta\notin\mathbb{N}, then β>α\beta>\alpha.

Remark 2.7.

If (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a tensor pair, and f,g:ℕ→ℕf,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, then (f⁡(α),g⁡(β))(f(\alpha),g(\beta)) is a tensor pair.

In this paper, we focus on the relationship between tensor products and Ramsey’s witnesses, which is grounded on the following fact. Its proof is implicit in the usual ultrafilter proof of Theorem (Ramsey’s Theorem for pairs)., see e.g. [CK90, Theorem 3.3.7]; below, we make it explicit for the reader’s convenience.

Proposition 2.8.

Let u∈β​ℕu\in\beta\mathbb{N} be a nonprincipal ultrafilter. Then u⊗u∈RWu\otimes u\in\mathrm{RW}.

Proof.

For A⊆ℕ2A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2} and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, write An≔{m∣(n,m)∈A}A_{n}\coloneqq\{m\mid(n,m)\in A\}, and let Au≔{n∣An∈u}A_{u}\coloneqq\{n\mid A_{n}\in u\}. By definition, A∈u⊗u⇔Au∈uA\in u\otimes u\iff A_{u}\in u. Fix A∈u⊗uA\in u\otimes u. We construct inductively an increasing sequence (xi)i∈ℕ(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} such that, for each ii, we have Axi∈uA_{x_{i}}\in u, and if i<ji<j then (xi,xj)∈A(x_{i},x_{j})\in A. To construct xk+1x_{k+1}, given x1<…<xk{x}_{1}<\ldots<{x}_{k}, we observe that the set Au∩⋂i≤kAxiA_{u}\cap\bigcap_{i\leq k}A_{x_{i}} belongs to uu, hence is infinite, so it contains some xk+1>xkx_{k+1}>x_{k}. ∎

Therefore, all products u⊗uu\otimes u with uu nonprincipal are Ramsey’s witnesses. Actually, we can be more precise: the set RW\mathrm{RW} is the closure of the set of such products. Recall that the topology on β​ℕk\beta\mathbb{N}^{k} has as basic clopen sets those of the form {u∈β​ℕk∣A∈u}\{u\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{k}\mid A\in u\}, for A⊆ℕkA\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{k}.

Definition 2.9.

We define the set of tensor squares as TS≔{u⊗u∈β​ℕ2∣u∈β​ℕ∖ℕ}\mathrm{TS}\coloneqq\{u\otimes u\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}\mid u\in\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}\}. We adopt similar conventions as in Definition 1.2, e.g. write (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} when 𝔲⁡(α,β)∈TS\tp(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathrm{TS}.

Theorem 2.10.

The topological closure TS¯\overline{\mathrm{TS}} coincides with RW\mathrm{RW}.

Proof.

It is clear from Definition 1.2 that RW\mathrm{RW} is a closed subset of β​ℕ2\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}, and it contains every u⊗uu\otimes u by Proposition 2.8, so it clearly includes TS¯\overline{\mathrm{TS}}. Conversely, let u∈RWu\in\mathrm{RW}, fix X∈uX\in u, and choose an infinite H⊆ℕH\subseteq\mathbb{N} with [H]2⊆X[H]^{2}\subseteq X. For h∈Hh\in H let Hh={x∈H∣x>h}H_{h}=\{x\in H\mid x>h\}; the family {Hh∣h∈H}\{H_{h}\mid h\in H\} has the FIP, and furthermore every finite intersection of this family is infinite. Therefore, it can be extended to a nonprincipal ultrafilter vv. For every h∈Hh\in H the fiber ([H]2)h=Hh([H]^{2})_{h}=H_{h} belongs to vv, and so H={n∈ℕ∣([H]2)n∈v}∈vH=\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid([H]^{2})_{n}\in v\}\in v, i.e. X⊇[H]2∈v⊗vX\supseteq[H]^{2}\in v\otimes v. ∎

We will need the following slight strengthening of Fact 2.4(2).

Proposition 2.11.

Let f,g:ℕn→ℕlf,g:\mathbb{N}^{n}\to\mathbb{N}^{l}. If gg is bounded-to-one, i.e. there is k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that every fiber of gg has size at most kk, and f⁡(α)∼g⁡(α)f(\alpha)\sim g(\alpha), then f⁡(α)=g⁡(α)f(\alpha)=g(\alpha).

Proof.

Without loss of generality α∉ℕn\alpha\notin\mathbb{N}^{n}, otherwise the conclusion trivially holds.

If gg is bijective, then by Fact 2.4(1) α∼g−1​(f​(α))\alpha\sim g^{-1}(f(\alpha)), so it suffices to apply Fact 2.4(2) to g−1∘fg^{-1}\circ f. The general case can be reduced to that of a bijection as follows.

For i≤ki\leq k, let Ci⊆ℕnC_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{n} be the set of those a∈ℕna\in\mathbb{N}^{n} that are the ii-th point of g−1​(g​(a))g^{-1}(g(a)) in the lexicographical order. Let ii be such that α∈∗Ci\alpha\in{}^{\ast}C_{i}. By repeatedly splitting CiC_{i} and selecting the piece belonging to 𝔲⁡(α)\tp(\alpha), we now find some C∈𝔲⁡(α)C\in\tp(\alpha) such that C⊆CiC\subseteq C_{i} and all of Ci∖CC_{i}\setminus C, g⁡(C)g(C) and g⁡(ℕn∖C)g(\mathbb{N}^{n}\setminus C) are infinite. By a routine argument, there is a bijective hh that agrees with gg on CC, and in particular h⁡(α)=g⁡(α)h(\alpha)=g(\alpha), which reduces the problem to the case above. ∎

Proposition 2.12.

Let α,β∈∗ℕ∖ℕ\alpha,\beta\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\mathbb{N}. The following properties hold.

  1. 1.

    (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} if and only if, for all A⊆ℕ2A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}, if (α,β)∈A∗(\alpha,\beta)\in{}^{\ast}{A} then there exists a pair (γ,δ)∈A∗(\gamma,\delta)\in{}^{\ast}{A} with (γ,δ)⊧TS(\gamma,\delta)\models\mathrm{TS}.

  2. 2.

    If (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} and f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} is such that f⁡(α)≠f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\neq f(\beta) then (f⁡(α),f⁡(β))⊧TS(f(\alpha),f(\beta))\models\mathrm{TS}.

  3. 3.

    If (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} and g:ℕ→ℕg:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} is such that g⁡(β)≠g⁡(α)g(\beta)\neq g(\alpha), then for all f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} g⁡(β)>f⁡(α)g(\beta)>f(\alpha).

Proof.
  1. 1.

    This is just a reformulation of Theorem 2.10 in terms of generators.

  2. 2.

    By Remark 2.7 (f⁡(α),f⁡(β))(f(\alpha),f(\beta)) is a tensor pair, and by Fact 2.4(1) f⁡(α)∼f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\sim f(\beta). This, together with f⁡(α)≠f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\neq f(\beta), implies f⁡(α)∉ℕf(\alpha)\notin\mathbb{N}, hence the conclusion.

  3. 3.

    By Remark 2.7 (f⁡(α),g⁡(β))(f(\alpha),g(\beta)) is a tensor pair. As g⁡(β)≠g⁡(α)g(\beta)\neq g(\alpha) and β∼α\beta\sim\alpha, we must have g⁡(β)∉ℕg(\beta)\notin\mathbb{N}, hence we conclude by Remark 2.6.∎

Proposition 2.13 (Properties of Ramsey pairs).

Let (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and f,g:ℕ→ℕf,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}. The following properties hold.

  1. 1.

    If f⁡(α)≠f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\neq f(\beta) then (f⁡(α),f⁡(β))⊧RW(f(\alpha),f(\beta))\models\mathrm{RW}.

  2. 2.

    If g⁡(α)≠g⁡(β)g(\alpha)\neq g(\beta), then f⁡(α)<g⁡(β)f(\alpha)<g(\beta).

  3. 3.

    Either f⁡(α)=f⁡(β)f(\alpha)=f(\beta) or α<f⁡(β)\alpha<f(\beta).

  4. 4.

    f⁡(α)<βf(\alpha)<\beta. In particular α<β\alpha<\beta.

  5. 5.

    If P,Q∈ℤ⁡[x]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x], with QQ of degree at least 11, then |P⁡(α)|<|Q⁡(β)|\lvert P(\alpha)\rvert<\lvert Q(\beta)\rvert.

  6. 6.

    If gg is finite-to-one, then f⁡(α)<g⁡(β)f(\alpha)<g(\beta).

  7. 7.

    α∼β\alpha\sim\beta.

Proof.
  1. 1.

    Fix A∈𝔲⁡(f⁡(α),f⁡(β))A\in\tp(f(\alpha),f(\beta)) and let B=(f,f)−1​(A)∩{(a,b)∣f⁡(a)≠f⁡(b)}B=(f,f)^{-1}(A)\cap\{(a,b)\mid f(a)\neq f(b)\}. By assumption, (α,β)∈B∗(\alpha,\beta)\in{}^{\ast}B, so by Proposition 2.12(1) there exists (γ,δ)∈B∗(\gamma,\delta)\in{}^{\ast}B with (γ,δ)⊧TS(\gamma,\delta)\models\mathrm{TS}. As f⁡(γ)≠f⁡(δ)f(\gamma)\neq f(\delta), the pair (f(γ),f(δ))∈A∗(f(\gamma),f(\delta))\in{}^{\ast}{A} satisfies (f⁡(γ),f⁡(δ))⊧TS(f(\gamma),f(\delta))\models\mathrm{TS} by Proposition 2.12(2). We conclude by Proposition 2.12(1).

  2. 2.

    For fixed f,gf,g, the set {(x,y)∣g⁡(x)≠g⁡(y)→f⁡(x)<g⁡(y)}\{(x,y)\mid g(x)\neq g(y)\to f(x)<g(y)\} belongs to every element of TS\mathrm{TS} by Proposition 2.12(3). The conclusion then follows by Theorem 2.10.

  3. 3.

    Immediate from 2.

  4. 4.

    This is a special case of 2.

  5. 5.

    This too is a special case of 2.

  6. 6.

    This follows by applying 4 to the function h⁡(n)≔max⁡g−1​([1,f⁡(n)])h(n)\coloneqq\max g^{-1}([1,f(n)]), which is well-defined because gg is finite-to-one.

  7. 7.

    Equivalence of α\alpha and β\beta is a closed condition and holds on TS\mathrm{TS}, so we conclude by Theorem 2.10.∎

Theorem 2.10 allows us to give a nonstandard description of RW\mathrm{RW}, Theorem 2.16 below, that makes use of internal ultrafilters, that is, elements of (βℕk)∗{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}^{k}).

Definition 2.14.

Let 𝔲∈(βℕ2)∗\mathfrak{u}\in{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}). We let st(𝔲)≔{A⊆ℕ2∣A∗∈𝔲}∈βℕ2\st(\mathfrak{u})\coloneqq\{A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}\mid{}^{\ast}{A}\in\mathfrak{u}\}\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}.

Remark 2.15.

The notation st⁡(𝔲)\st(\mathfrak{u}) is consistent with viewing (βℕ2)∗{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}) topologically as a nonstandard extension of β​ℕ2\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}, namely st⁡(𝔲)=u\st(\mathfrak{u})=u if and only if 𝔲∈∗A\mathfrak{u}\in{}^{\ast}{A} for all neighbourhoods AA of uu.

Below, we abuse the notation and write ⊗\otimes for the nonstandard extension of ⊗\otimes to (βℕ2)∗{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}^{2}).

Theorem 2.16.

v∈RWv\in\mathrm{RW} if and only if there is 𝔲∈(βℕ∖ℕ)∗\mathfrak{u}\in{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}) such that v=st⁡(𝔲⊗𝔲)v=\st(\mathfrak{u}\otimes\mathfrak{u}).

Proof.

This is a special case of the nonstandard characterisation of topological closure, but we spell out some details for the reader’s convenience.

Left to right, for X⊆ℕ2X\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}, define

ΛX≔{u∈β​ℕ∖ℕ∣X∈u⊗u}.\Lambda_{X}\coloneqq\{u\in\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}\mid X\in u\otimes u\}.

By assumption and Theorem 2.10, for each X∈vX\in v the set ΛX\Lambda_{X} is nonempty. In fact, the family {ΛX∣X∈v}\{\Lambda_{X}\mid X\in v\} has the FIP, and it follows that there is 𝔲∈(βℕ∖ℕ)∗\mathfrak{u}\in{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}) such that, for every X∈vX\in v we have ∗X∈𝔲⊗𝔲{}^{\ast}X\in\mathfrak{u}\otimes\mathfrak{u}. This implies that st⁡(𝔲⊗𝔲)=v\st(\mathfrak{u}\otimes\mathfrak{u})=v.

Right to left, let 𝔲∈(βℕ∖ℕ)∗\mathfrak{u}\in{}^{\ast}(\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}). By transfer, for every internal B⊆∗ℕ2B\subseteq{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{2} such that B∈𝔲⊗𝔲B\in\mathfrak{u}\otimes\mathfrak{u}, there is a ∗infinite H⊆∗ℕH\subseteq{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} such that [H]2⊆B[H]^{2}\subseteq B. In particular, this applies to those BB of the form ∗X{}^{\ast}X for X⊆ℕ2X\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}. By applying downward transfer to the formula “there is a ∗infinite H⊆∗ℕH\subseteq{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} such that [H]2⊆X∗[H]^{2}\subseteq{}^{\ast}X”, we find an infinite K⊆ℕK\subseteq\mathbb{N} such that [K]2⊆X[K]^{2}\subseteq X. It follows that st⁡(𝔲⊗𝔲)∈RW\st(\mathfrak{u}\otimes\mathfrak{u})\in\mathrm{RW}. ∎

Proposition 2.17.

If (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) is a tensor triple, β∼γ\beta\sim\gamma, and f:ℕ2→ℕf:\mathbb{N}^{2}\to\mathbb{N}, is such that f⁡(α,β)≠f⁡(α,γ)f(\alpha,\beta)\neq f(\alpha,\gamma), then (f⁡(α,β),f⁡(α,γ))⊧RW(f(\alpha,\beta),f(\alpha,\gamma))\models\mathrm{RW}.

Proof.

Given A∈𝔲⁡(f⁡(α,β),f⁡(α,γ))A\in\tp(f(\alpha,\beta),f(\alpha,\gamma)), we need to find an element of TS\mathrm{TS} containing AA. By associativity, the pair (α,(β,γ))(\alpha,(\beta,\gamma)) is tensor, hence by Fact 2.2 and assumption there is n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that A∈𝔲⁡(f⁡(n,β),f⁡(n,γ))A\in\tp(f(n,\beta),f(n,\gamma)) and f⁡(n,β)≠f⁡(n,γ)f(n,\beta)\neq f(n,\gamma). The latter, together with (β,γ)⊧TS(\beta,\gamma)\models\mathrm{TS}, gives us by Proposition 2.12(2) that (f⁡(n,β),f⁡(n,γ))⊧TS(f(n,\beta),f(n,\gamma))\models\mathrm{TS}, hence the conclusion. ∎

Fact 2.5 combined with Proposition 2.17 allows us to build explicit Ramsey pairs that are not tensor pairs.

Example 2.18.

Let u,v∈β​ℕu,v\in\beta\mathbb{N} be non-principal and let w∈β​ℕ2w\in\beta\mathbb{N}^{2} be the image (or pushforward) of u⊗v⊗vu\otimes v\otimes v under the function h:ℕ3→ℕ2h:\mathbb{N}^{3}\to\mathbb{N}^{2} defined as h⁡(x,y,z)=(2x​3y,2x​3z)h(x,y,z)=(2^{x}3^{y},2^{x}3^{z}). That is, for all A⊆ℕ2A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}

A∈w⇔{(a,b,c)∣(2a​3b,2a​3c)∈A}∈u⊗v⊗v.A\in w\Leftrightarrow\{(a,b,c)\mid(2^{a}3^{b},2^{a}3^{c})\in A\}\in u\otimes v\otimes v.

To check that w∈RWw\in\mathrm{RW}, let (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) be a generator of u⊗v⊗vu\otimes v\otimes v; so (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) is a tensor triple and β∼γ\beta\sim\gamma. Therefore, by Proposition 2.17 we have (2α​3β,2α​3γ)⊧RW(2^{\alpha}3^{\beta},2^{\alpha}3^{\gamma})\models\mathrm{RW}, and by Fact 2.5 applied with the 22-adic valuation we obtain (2α​3β,2α​3γ) ／⊧TS(2^{\alpha}3^{\beta},2^{\alpha}3^{\gamma})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\models}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\models}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.625pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\models}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.875pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\models}}}\mathrm{TS}.

Remark 2.19.

By Example 2.18 the inclusion TS⊆RW\mathrm{TS}\subseteq\mathrm{RW} is strict, hence TS\mathrm{TS} is not closed.

In this paper, we are not going to study general properties of block partition regularity; in fact, as said in the introduction, we are mainly interested to use Ramsey pairs to study “infinitary statements” in combinatorics close in spirit to Theorem (Ramsey’s Theorem for pairs).. “Infinitary statements” is a vague concept, that could be formalised in several different ways; in this paper, we define it as the following strengthening of block partition regularity:

  4. 4.

    The analogue of Remark 3.4 holds also for Ramsey partition regularity, provided one does not split (x,y)(x,y) into separate blocks.

In Section 4, we will see which of the above partition regularity notions are satisfied by an important and well-studied example, namely the formula

φ⁡(x,y,z,t)≔(x+y=z)∧(x⋅y=t)∧x≠y.\varphi(x,y,z,t)\coloneqq(x+y=z)\wedge(x\cdot y=t)\wedge x\neq y.

As recalled in the introduction, partition regularity problems can be rephrased both in ultrafilters and in nonstandard terms. The main result of this section is the analogous characterisation of Ramsey partition regularity, which will be central for our applications.
