Theorem 3.8 reduces Ramsey partition regularity problems to existence problems for Ramsey pairs with certain combinatorial properties. We are going to exploit this idea, look at formulas of the form ⋀i≤nfi​(x,y)=zi\bigwedge_{i\leq n}f_{i}(x,y)=z_{i}, and study their Ramsey partition regularity in (x,y)|z1,…,zn(x,y)\mid{z}_{1},\ldots,{z}_{n}. By Theorem 3.8, this can be rephrased as follows.

Corollary 3.9.

Let f1,…,fn:ℕ2→ℕf_{1},\ldots,f_{n}:\mathbb{N}^{2}\to\mathbb{N}. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    The formula ⋀i≤nfi​(x,y)=zi\bigwedge_{i\leq n}f_{i}(x,y)=z_{i} is Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z1,…,zn(x,y)\mid{z}_{1},\ldots,{z}_{n}.

  2. 2.

    There is a Ramsey pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) such that f1​(α,β)∼…∼fn​(α,β)f_{1}(\alpha,\beta)\sim\ldots\sim f_{n}(\alpha,\beta).

  3. 3.

    There is w∈RWw\in\mathrm{RW} such that f1​(w)=…=fn​(w)f_{1}(w)=\ldots=f_{n}(w).

Note that, if one of the fif_{i} is the projection on the first (or second) coordinate, then we are actually studying the Ramsey partition regularity in (x,y),z1,…,zn(x,y),{z}_{1},\ldots,{z}_{n}. One might wonder whether, in condition 3, RW\mathrm{RW} could be strengthened to TS\mathrm{TS}. This is not the case, as we will see in Remark 5.13.

4 Pairwise sums and products: a case study

In the language introduced in this paper, the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem). says that the formula φ⁡(x,y,z,t)≔(x+y=z)∧(x⋅y=t)\varphi(x,y,z,t)\coloneqq(x+y=z)\wedge(x\cdot y=t) is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t. By Corollary 3.9 this is, in disguise, a result about Ramsey pairs, namely the following.

Theorem 4.1.

Let (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}. Then α+β≁α​β\alpha+\beta\nsim\alpha\beta.

We show how our techniques can be used to give a short nonstandard proof of this, and in fact prove a much stronger result. Let us begin by fixing some notation.

Definition 4.2.

Let p,m∈ℕ∖{1}p,m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}, with pp prime. We denote by vpv_{p} the pp-adic valuation, and we let ℓm​(x)≔⌊logm⁡(x)⌋\ell_{m}(x)\coloneqq\lfloor\log_{m}(x)\rfloor, both regarded as functions ℕ→ℕ∪{0}\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}. We denote by smodp:ℕ→{1,…,p−1}\smod_{p}:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,p-1\} the function that maps xx to x/pvp​(x)modpx/p^{v_{p}(x)}\mod p.

When p,mp,m are clear from context, we write ℓ,v,smod\ell,v,\smod for brevity.

Note that, if xx is written in base pp, and we count digit positions right to left44 4 So “first” means “least significant”. and starting from 00, then vp​(x)v_{p}(x) is the position of the first nonzero digit, smodp⁡(x)\smod_{p}(x) is that digit, and ℓp​(x)\ell_{p}(x) is the position of the last nonzero digit.

Lemma 4.3.

Let n,m∈ℤ∖{0}n,m\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\} with n+m≠0n+m\neq 0 and p>|n|+|m|p>\lvert n\rvert+\lvert m\rvert a standard prime. If α∼β\alpha\sim\beta and vp​(α)≤vp​(β)v_{p}(\alpha)\leq v_{p}(\beta), then vp​(n​α+m​β)=vp​(α)v_{p}(n\alpha+m\beta)=v_{p}(\alpha).

Proof.

Write v≔vpv\coloneqq v_{p} and smod≔smodp\smod\coloneqq\smod_{p}. If v⁡(α)<v⁡(β)v(\alpha)<v(\beta) we conclude by basic valuation theory and the fact that p∤np\nmid n, so we may assume that v⁡(α)=v⁡(β)v(\alpha)=v(\beta). Observe that v⁡(n​α+m​β)≥v⁡(α)v(n\alpha+m\beta)\geq v(\alpha). Moreover, as smod\smod has finite image and α∼β\alpha\sim\beta, we have smod⁡(α)=smod⁡(β)\smod(\alpha)=\smod(\beta), hence the digit in position v⁡(α)v(\alpha) of n​α+m​βn\alpha+m\beta is (n+m)​smod⁡(α)modp(n+m)\smod(\alpha)\mod p, which is not 00 by the assumptions on pp and n+mn+m. ∎

The main result of this section is the following:

Theorem 4.4.

Let (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and f,g:ℕ→ℤf,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}. Then, provided that f⁡(α),g⁡(α)∉ℤf(\alpha),g(\alpha)\notin\mathbb{Z},

(f⁡(α)+f⁡(β),g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))≁(f⁡(α),g⁡(β)).(f(\alpha)+f(\beta),\>g(\alpha)+g(\beta))\nsim(f(\alpha),\>g(\beta)).

More generally, for every k1,k2,k3,k4∈ℤk_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}\in\mathbb{Z},

(f⁡(α)+f⁡(β)+k1,g⁡(α)+g⁡(β)+k2)≁(f⁡(α)+k3,g⁡(β)+k4).(f(\alpha)+f(\beta)+k_{1},\;g(\alpha)+g(\beta)+k_{2})\nsim(f(\alpha)+k_{3},\>g(\beta)+k_{4}).
Proof.

Up to replacing ff by −f-f, and similarly for gg, we may assume that f⁡(α),g⁡(α)>ℕf(\alpha),g(\alpha)>\mathbb{N}. By Fact 2.4(1), by replacing ff by f+k3−k1f+k_{3}-k_{1} and gg by g+k4−k2g+k_{4}-k_{2} we may assume that k1=k3k_{1}=k_{3} and k2=k4k_{2}=k_{4}. By applying (id−k1,id−k2)(\id-k_{1},\id-k_{2}) we then reduce to the case k1,k2,k3,k4=0k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4}=0.

Suppose that (f⁡(α)+f⁡(β),g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))∼(f⁡(α),g⁡(β))(f(\alpha)+f(\beta),\>g(\alpha)+g(\beta))\sim(f(\alpha),\;g(\beta)). Fix a prime p>2p>2 and, for brevity, let v≔vpv\coloneqq v_{p}, and similarly for ℓ\ell and smod\smod.

Observe that v⁡(f⁡(α))≠v⁡(f⁡(β))v(f(\alpha))\neq v(f(\beta)); in fact, by assumption f⁡(α),f⁡(β)≠0f(\alpha),f(\beta)\neq 0 and, if they had different valuation, because p>2p>2 and f⁡(α)∼f⁡(β)f(\alpha)\sim f(\beta), we would have smod⁡(f⁡(α)+f⁡(β))≡2​smod⁡(f⁡(α))(modp)\smod(f(\alpha)+f(\beta))\equiv 2\smod(f(\alpha))\pmod{p}, contradicting f⁡(α)+f⁡(β)∼f⁡(α)f(\alpha)+f(\beta)\sim f(\alpha).

Thus, since (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}, by Proposition 2.13(2) we have v⁡(f⁡(β))>ℕ(α)v(f(\beta))>\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha). Similarly, v⁡(g⁡(β))>ℕ(α)v(g(\beta))>\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha), which implies v⁡(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β))=v⁡(g⁡(α))v(g(\alpha)+g(\beta))=v(g(\alpha)). Now observe that

ℓ⁡(f⁡(α)+f⁡(β))≥v⁡(f⁡(β))>ℓ⁡(g⁡(α))+1>v⁡(g⁡(α))=v⁡(g⁡(α)+g⁡(β)).\ell(f(\alpha)+f(\beta))\geq v(f(\beta))>\ell(g(\alpha))+1>v(g(\alpha))=v(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)).

As the pairs are equivalent, it follows that ℓ⁡(f⁡(α))>v⁡(g⁡(β))\ell(f(\alpha))>v(g(\beta)), against v⁡(g⁡(β))>ℕ(α)v(g(\beta))>\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha). ∎

Theorem 4.1 can now be deduced from Theorem 4.4 as follows.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Suppose by contradiction this is the case, fix a sufficiently large standard prime pp and write v≔vpv\coloneqq v_{p} and similarly for ℓ\ell and smod\smod. By applying the function (v,ℓ)(v,\ell) we get (v⁡(α​β),ℓ⁡(α​β))∼(v⁡(α+β),ℓ⁡(α+β))(v(\alpha\beta),\;\ell(\alpha\beta))\sim(v(\alpha+\beta),\;\ell(\alpha+\beta)). We have

  • •

    v⁡(α​β)=v⁡(α)+v⁡(β)v(\alpha\beta)=v(\alpha)+v(\beta).

  • •

    ℓ⁡(α​β)=ℓ⁡(α)+ℓ⁡(β)+ε\ell(\alpha\beta)=\ell(\alpha)+\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon with ε∈{0,1}\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}.

  • •

    v⁡(α+β)=v⁡(α)v(\alpha+\beta)=v(\alpha): in fact, v⁡(α)≤v⁡(β)v(\alpha)\leq v(\beta) by Proposition 2.13(2), so we may apply Lemma 4.3.

  • •

    ℓ⁡(α+β)=ℓ⁡(β)+ε′\ell(\alpha+\beta)=\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon^{\prime} with ε′∈{0,1}\varepsilon^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}.

Thus (v⁡(α)+v⁡(β),ℓ⁡(α)+ℓ⁡(β)+ε)∼(v⁡(α),ℓ⁡(β)+ε′)(v(\alpha)+v(\beta),\;\ell(\alpha)+\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon)\sim(v(\alpha),\;\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon^{\prime}), and since ℓ⁡(α)>ℕ\ell(\alpha)>\mathbb{N} Theorem 4.4 implies that v⁡(α)∈ℕ∪{0}v(\alpha)\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.

The ultrafilter 𝔲⁡(α)\tp(\alpha) determines, for each power pkp^{k}, a remainder class modulo pkp^{k}. In other words, it determines the pp-adic class a∈ℤpa\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} of α\alpha. Therefore, since α​β∼α+β\alpha\beta\sim\alpha+\beta we obtain a2=2​aa^{2}=2a in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}. Because we proved above that v⁡(α)∈ℕ∪{0}v(\alpha)\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, it follows that a=2a=2.

The pair (γ,δ)≔(α−2,β−2)(\gamma,\delta)\coloneqq(\alpha-2,\beta-2) is Ramsey by Proposition 2.13(1), and α​β∼α+β\alpha\beta\sim\alpha+\beta yields

γ​δ+2​(γ+δ)∼γ+δ.\gamma\delta+2(\gamma+\delta)\sim\gamma+\delta. (1)

As α∉ℕ\alpha\notin\mathbb{N} we have γ≠0\gamma\neq 0, and since the class of γ\gamma in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} is 00 it follows that v⁡(γ)>ℕv(\gamma)>\mathbb{N}. By Lemma 4.3 and the fact that p>2p>2,

v⁡(γ​δ)>v⁡(γ)=v⁡(γ+δ)=v⁡(2​(γ+δ)).v(\gamma\delta)>v(\gamma)=v(\gamma+\delta)=v(2(\gamma+\delta)).

Therefore, smod⁡(γ​δ+2​(γ+δ))=smod⁡(2​(γ+δ))\smod(\gamma\delta+2(\gamma+\delta))=\smod(2(\gamma+\delta)), contradicting (1). ∎

Let us observe that, with the same idea as in the proof of Theorem 4.4, one proves the following.

Remark 4.5.

Let (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}. For every f,g,h,kf,g,h,k, if there are φ,ψ\varphi,\psi such that φ⁡(g⁡(β))≠φ⁡(g⁡(α))\varphi(g(\beta))\neq\varphi(g(\alpha)) and φ⁡(k⁡(α,β))≤ψ⁡(h⁡(α,β))\varphi(k(\alpha,\beta))\leq\psi(h(\alpha,\beta)), then (h⁡(α,β),k⁡(α,β))≁(f⁡(α),g⁡(β))(h(\alpha,\beta),k(\alpha,\beta))\nsim(f(\alpha),g(\beta)). Otherwise we get φ⁡(g⁡(β))>ℕ(α)\varphi(g(\beta))>\mathop{\mathbb{N}}(\alpha), and in particular φ⁡(g⁡(β))>ψ⁡(f⁡(α))\varphi(g(\beta))>\psi(f(\alpha)), against φ⁡(k⁡(α,β))≤ψ⁡(h⁡(α,β))\varphi(k(\alpha,\beta))\leq\psi(h(\alpha,\beta)).

Theorem 4.1 says that the formula

φ⁡(x,y,z,t)≔(x+y=z)∧(x⋅y=t)∧x≠y.\varphi(x,y,z,t)\coloneqq(x+y=z)\wedge(x\cdot y=t)\wedge x\neq y.

is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t. We now look at its other block and Ramsey partition regularity properties.

As known, the partition regularity of φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) is one of the major open problems in this area of combinatorics. It has been recently solved over ℚ\mathbb{Q} [BS24]; see also [Alw24] for an extension to finite arbitrarily large sums and products. On ℕ\mathbb{N}, the most general result we are aware of is the following theorem proven by J. Moreira in [Mor17, Corollary 1.5], which we state here using the language of block partition regularity.

Theorem 4.6 (Moreira).

φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) is BPR in x,z,t|yx,z,t\mid y.

Moreira’s Theorem, together with some basic considerations, solves most block partition regularity problems for φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t). We list the problems and their status in Table 1. We write “Never considered” when we are not aware of any work on the problem and, for compactness, we use the following observation.

Remark 4.7.

We may omit redundant choices of blocks, arising from the symmetry in x,yx,y of the formula φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t), or from the fact that variables inside a block can be permuted.

The picture is much richer when it comes to the different kinds of Ramsey partition regularity one might ask for φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t). First, we summarise what happens when variables in the “Ramsey part” are in a block of their own. Three such cases need some simple computations to be carried out, which we do in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.8.

The formula φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) is Ramsey PR in (x,t)​∣y∣​z(x,t)\mid y\mid z and (x,z)​∣y∣​t(x,z)\mid y\mid t, but it is not Ramsey PR in (z,t)​∣x∣​y(z,t)\mid x\mid y.

Proof.

For the Ramsey partition regularity in (x,t)​∣y∣​z(x,t)\mid y\mid z, fix (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and let (x,t)=(2α,2β)(x,t)=(2^{\alpha},2^{\beta}), while y=2β−αy=2^{\beta-\alpha} and z=2α+2β−αz=2^{\alpha}+2^{\beta-\alpha}.

For the Ramsey partition regularity in (x,z)​∣y∣​t(x,z)\mid y\mid t, fix any (x,z)=(α,β)⊧RW(x,z)=(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and let y=β−αy=\beta-\alpha and t=α⋅(β−α)t=\alpha\cdot(\beta-\alpha).

For the non Ramsey partition regularity in (z,t)​∣x∣​y(z,t)\mid x\mid y, assume by contrast that there are (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ,δ∈∗ℕ\gamma,\delta\in{}^{\ast}\mathbb{N} such that α=γ+δ\alpha=\gamma+\delta and β=γ​δ\beta=\gamma\delta. Then α2=(γ+δ)2=γ2+2​γ​δ+δ2>γ​δ=β\alpha^{2}=(\gamma+\delta)^{2}=\gamma^{2}+2\gamma\delta+\delta^{2}>\gamma\delta=\beta, against Proposition 2.13(4). ∎

Table 2 lists all the cases where the “Ramsey part” is in a block of its own, except those excluded by Remark 4.7 or by the following Remark 4.9.

Remark 4.9.

We may omit cases containing (z,x)(z,x), (t,x)(t,x) or (t,z)(t,z) which, if there were a pair (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} witnessing Ramsey PR, would yield α+β<α\alpha+\beta<\alpha, α⋅β<α\alpha\cdot\beta<\alpha, and α⋅β<α+β\alpha\cdot\beta<\alpha+\beta respectively.

Finally, we are left to consider the cases where variables in the “Ramsey part” share a block with other variables. Some such cases can be easily proven by simple computations.

Lemma 4.10.

The formula φ⁡(x,y,z,t)\varphi(x,y,z,t) is Ramsey PR in (x,z),y|t(x,z),y\mid t and (x,t),y|z(x,t),y\mid z.

Proof.

Let (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) be a tensor triple of infinite equivalent elements.

For the (x,z),y|t(x,z),y\mid t case we let x=β−αx=\beta-\alpha, z=γ−αz=\gamma-\alpha, y=γ−βy=\gamma-\beta and t=(β−α)​(γ−β)t=\left(\beta-\alpha\right)\left(\gamma-\beta\right).

For the (x,t),y|z(x,t),y\mid z case we additionally require that α\alpha is divisible by all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and we let x=β/α,t=γ/α,y=γ/βx=\beta/\alpha,t=\gamma/\alpha,y=\gamma/\beta and z=(β/α)+(γ/β)z=\left(\beta/\alpha\right)+\left(\gamma/\beta\right). ∎

We use Lemma 4.10 to list all remaining cases in Table 3, again with the omissions arising from Remarks 4.7 and 4.9.

5 Ramsey PR of equations

In this section we apply the characterisations obtained in Corollary 3.9 to study the Ramsey partition regularity of several equations. We begin with polynomial ones. The two-variable case is trivial, for the following reason.

Fact 5.1.

If α∼β\alpha\sim\beta are infinite, then P⁡(α,β)=0P(\alpha,\beta)=0 if and only if α=β\alpha=\beta and P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) is a multiple of (x−y)(x-y).

Proof.

By [ALB24, Corollary 3.2] and Fact 1.1. ∎

Proposition 5.2.

No two-variable polynomial equation is Ramsey PR.

Proof.

We use Fact 5.1. Since every Ramsey pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) satisfies α<β\alpha<\beta and α∼β\alpha\sim\beta (Proposition 2.13, points 2 and 7 respectively), no such pair can satisfy the formula P⁡(x,y)=0P(x,y)=0. ∎

We start our discussion by fixing some notations and proving some simple, yet useful, general result.

Definition 5.3.

For P⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]P(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x], we let deg⁡(P)\deg(P) be its degree and c⁡(P)c(P) be its leading coefficient.

When evaluating polynomials at infinite points, it is natural to consider the following notion:

Definition 5.4.

Let α,β∈∗ℕ\alpha,\beta\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}. We say that α,β\alpha,\beta are in the same archimedean class, and write α≍β\alpha\asymp\beta, if there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that (1/n)≤(α/β)≤n(1/n)\leq(\alpha/\beta)\leq n. We write α≪β\alpha\ll\beta if the archimedean class of α\alpha is strictly smaller than that of β\beta, that is, if for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have n⋅α<βn\cdot\alpha<\beta.

A related way to think about ≍\asymp is the following: let us recall that a hyperreal ρ∈∗ℝ\rho\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{R}} is called finite if there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such |ρ|≤n|\rho|\leq n. In this case, ρ\rho admits a standard part, denoted by st⁡(ρ)\st(\rho) and defined as the unique standard real rr whose distance from ρ\rho is infinitesimal, i.e. smaller than 1/n1/n for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Saying α≍β\alpha\asymp\beta means saying that α/β\alpha/\beta is finite and its standard part is not 00, while saying that α≪β\alpha\ll\beta means that st⁡(α/β)=0\st(\alpha/\beta)=0.

By Fact 2.4(2), if α∼β\alpha\sim\beta and q∈ℚq\in\mathbb{Q}, then α=q​β\alpha=q\beta forces q=1q=1. The first part of next lemma is a simple generalisation of this fact where == is replaced by ≍\asymp.

Lemma 5.5.

Let α∼β\alpha\sim\beta be infinite and P,Q∈ℤ⁡[x]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be polynomials of degrees deg⁡(P)=n\deg(P)=n and deg⁡(Q)=m\deg(Q)=m. If n,m≥1n,m\geq 1, then:

  1. 1.

    if α≍β\alpha\asymp\beta then st⁡(α/β)=1\st\left({\alpha}/{\beta}\right)=1;

  2. 2.

    if P⁡(α)≍Q⁡(β)P(\alpha)\asymp Q(\beta) then n=mn=m;

  3. 3.

    if P⁡(α)∼Q⁡(β)P(\alpha)\sim Q(\beta) then P=QP=Q.

Proof.

Fix an arbitrary finite prime pp and let ℓ≔ℓp\ell\coloneqq\ell_{p}.

  1. 1.

    Write α,β\alpha,\beta in base pp. In the notations of our previous section, ℓ⁡(α)∼ℓ⁡(β)\ell(\alpha)\sim\ell(\beta). Hence either ℓ⁡(α)=ℓ⁡(β)\ell(\alpha)=\ell(\beta) or the value |ℓ⁡(α)−ℓ⁡(β)||\ell(\alpha)-\ell(\beta)| is infinite, and the latter is impossible as in this case α/β\alpha/\beta would either be infinite or infinitesimal, against our hypothesis. Let λ=ℓ⁡(α)=ℓ⁡(β)\lambda=\ell(\alpha)=\ell(\beta). As α∼β\alpha\sim\beta, for all finite ii the coefficients of pλ−ip^{\lambda-i} in the base pp expansions of α\alpha and β\beta coincide; then, by overspill, there exists an infinite τ\tau such that for every i≤τi\leq\tau the (λ−i)(\lambda-i)-th coefficient cλ−ic_{\lambda-i} in the base pp-expansions of α\alpha and β\beta is the same. Let γ=∑i=0τcλ−i​pλ−i\gamma=\sum_{i=0}^{\tau}c_{\lambda-i}p^{\lambda-i}. Then:

    • •

      α=γ+ε\alpha=\gamma+\varepsilon, with ε≪γ\varepsilon\ll\gamma;

    • •

      β=γ+ε′\beta=\gamma+\varepsilon^{\prime}, with ε′≪γ\varepsilon^{\prime}\ll\gamma.

    Hence α/β=(γ+ε)/(γ+ε′)\alpha/\beta=(\gamma+\varepsilon)/(\gamma+\varepsilon^{\prime}) has standard part 11.

  2. 2.

    First of all, we observe that

    αn≍P⁡(α)≍Q⁡(β)≍βm,\alpha^{n}\asymp P(\alpha)\asymp Q(\beta)\asymp\beta^{m},

    so αn≍βm\alpha^{n}\asymp\beta^{m}. Therefore, ℓ⁡(αn)\ell(\alpha^{n}) is at finite distance from ℓ⁡(βm)\ell(\beta^{m}), so there is a finite k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} such that n​ℓ​(α)+k=m​ℓ​(β)n\ell(\alpha)+k=m\ell(\beta). As ℓ⁡(α)∼ℓ⁡(β)\ell(\alpha)\sim\ell(\beta), if this happens then the equation n​x−m​y=knx-my=k is PR. By Rado’s Theorem, this can happen only when n=mn=m (and k=0k=0).

  3. 3.

    The assumptions imply P⁡(α)∼Q⁡(α)P(\alpha)\sim Q(\alpha). As polynomials are bounded-to-one, by Proposition 2.11 we must have P⁡(α)=Q⁡(α)P(\alpha)=Q(\alpha). So P⁡(α)−Q⁡(α)=0P(\alpha)-Q(\alpha)=0, and since α\alpha is infinite we must have P=QP=Q.∎

Lemma 5.5 allows some simple, yet interesting, observations. For instance, we may combine it with Rado’s Theorem and van der Waerden’s Theorem to obtain the following propositions.

Proposition 5.6.

Let a,b,c∈ℕa,b,c\in\mathbb{N}.

  1. 1.

    If a=c≠ba=c\neq b, then for all finite partitions ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} and all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, there exist i≤ri\leq r and x,y,z∈Cix,y,z\in C_{i} with x>N​yx>Ny and such that a​x+b​y=c​zax+by=cz. Moreover, the analogous result with x>N​yx>Ny replaced by y>N​xy>Nx is false.

  2. 2.

    If a+b=ca+b=c then for all finite partitions ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} and all ε>0\varepsilon>0 there are i≤ri\leq r and x,y,z∈Cix,y,z\in C_{i} with |(x/y)−1|,|(x/z)−1|<ε\lvert(x/y)-1\rvert,\lvert(x/z)-1\rvert<\varepsilon and such that a​x+b​y=c​zax+by=cz. Moreover, for all N>1N>1, there is a finite partition ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r} such that for all i≤ri\leq r and all x,y,z∈Cix,y,z\in C_{i} with x>N​yx>Ny we have a​x+b​y≠c​zax+by\neq cz. Similarly with x,yx,y replaced, in x>N​yx>Ny, by any two distinct elements of {x,y,z}\{x,y,z\}.

Proof.

By Rado’s Theorem, the equation a​x+b​y=c​zax+by=cz is PR if and only if a=ca=c, or b=cb=c, or a+b=ca+b=c. In nonstandard terms, this equation is PR if and only if there exist α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma such that a​α+b​β=c​γa\alpha+b\beta=c\gamma. Fix such α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma.

  1. 1.

    It suffices to show that β≪α\beta\ll\alpha. If α≍β\alpha\asymp\beta then a​α+b​β≍(a+b)​αa\alpha+b\beta\asymp(a+b)\alpha, so c​γ≍(a+b)​αc\gamma\asymp(a+b)\alpha, hence by Lemma 5.5(1) we should have a+b=ca+b=c, against the assumption. If α≪β\alpha\ll\beta, it similarly follows that b=cb=c.

  2. 2.

    It suffices to show that st⁡(α/β)=st⁡(β/γ)=1\st(\alpha/\beta)=\st(\beta/\gamma)=1, and by Lemma 5.5(1) it is enough to prove α≍β≍γ\alpha\asymp\beta\asymp\gamma. This follows easily from the equation a​α+b​β=(a+b)​γa\alpha+b\beta=(a+b)\gamma and again Lemma 5.5(1).∎

Proposition 5.7.

For every N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, every k>1k>1, and every finite partition ℕ=C1∪…∪Cr\mathbb{N}=C_{1}\cup\ldots\cup C_{r}, there exist i≤ri\leq r and x,y∈ℕx,y\in\mathbb{N} such that x>N​yx>Ny and for all 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k we have x+j​y∈Cix+jy\in C_{i}. Moreover, the analogous result with x>N​yx>Ny replaced by y>N​xy>Nx is false.

Proof.

By the nonstandard characterisation of van der Waerden’s Theorem there exists α,β\alpha,\beta such that for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have α∼α+n​β\alpha\sim\alpha+n\beta. Arguing as in the proof of Proposition 5.6 we deduce that β≪α\beta\ll\alpha. From this, the conclusion follows easily. ∎

The last technical result that we will need is the following:

Lemma 5.8.

Let P⁡(x),Q⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]P(x),Q(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be such that deg⁡(P)=deg⁡(Q)=d>1\deg(P)=\deg(Q)=d>1. Assume that c⁡(P),c⁡(Q)>0c(P),c(Q)>0 and let c≔c⁡(P)/c⁡(Q)c\coloneqq{c(P)}/{c(Q)}. For all β∈∗ℕ∖ℕ\beta\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\mathbb{N} there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that Q⁡(cd​β−n)≤P⁡(β)≤Q⁡(cd​β+n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta-n)\leq P(\beta)\leq Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta+n).

Proof.

Let c′​(P),c′​(Q)c^{\prime}(P),c^{\prime}(Q) be the coefficients of xd−1x^{d-1} in P,QP,Q respectively. Observe that, as β\beta is infinite, our hypotheses on P,QP,Q give us that Q⁡(cd​x−n),P⁡(x),Q⁡(cd​x+n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x-n),P(x),Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x+n) all have the same leading monomial, hence the inequality in the conclusion holds if and only if the same inequality holds for the coefficients of xd−1x^{d-1} in Q⁡(cd​x−n),P⁡(x),Q⁡(cd​x+n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x-n),P(x),Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x+n) respectively. This coefficient is (c′​(Q)−d​n⋅c⁡(Q))​cd−1d(c^{\prime}(Q)-dn\cdot c(Q))c^{\frac{d-1}{d}} in Q⁡(cd​x−n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x-n) and it is (c′​(Q)+d​n⋅c⁡(Q))​cd−1d(c^{\prime}(Q)+dn\cdot c(Q))c^{\frac{d-1}{d}} in Q⁡(cd​x+n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}x+n). To conclude, it suffices to find some nn such that

(c′​(Q)−d​n⋅c⁡(Q))​cd−1d≤c′​(P)≤(c′​(Q)+d​n⋅c⁡(Q))​cd−1d.(c^{\prime}(Q)-dn\cdot c(Q))c^{\frac{d-1}{d}}\leq c^{\prime}(P)\leq(c^{\prime}(Q)+dn\cdot c(Q))c^{\frac{d-1}{d}}.

Because d⋅c⁡(Q)d\cdot c(Q) and cc are positive, it is enough to take nn sufficiently large. ∎

We are now ready to discuss the Ramsey partition regularity of polynomial equations in three variables. Our first result is very general, as it involves arbitrary functions in xx.

Theorem 5.9.

Let P⁡(x),Q⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]P(x),Q(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be nonzero polynomials with P⁡(0)=Q⁡(0)=0P(0)=Q(0)=0. Let f:ℕ→ℤf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z} and let φ⁡(x,y,z)≔(f⁡(x)+P⁡(y)=Q⁡(z))∧(f⁡(x)≠0)\varphi(x,y,z)\coloneqq(f(x)+P(y)=Q(z))\land(f(x)\neq 0). If φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z then P=QP=Q and deg⁡(P)=1\deg(P)=1.

Proof.

Let dP=deg⁡(P),dQ=deg⁡(Q)d_{P}=\deg(P),d_{Q}=\deg(Q). By Theorem 3.8, as φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z there exist (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ∼α\gamma\sim\alpha such that f⁡(α)+P⁡(β)=Q⁡(γ)f(\alpha)+P(\beta)=Q(\gamma) and f⁡(α)≠0f(\alpha)\neq 0; note that, by Proposition 2.13(4), f⁡(α)≪βf(\alpha)\ll\beta. Hence

βdP≍f⁡(α)+P⁡(β)=Q⁡(γ)≍γdQ.\beta^{d_{P}}\asymp f(\alpha)+P(\beta)=Q(\gamma)\asymp\gamma^{d_{Q}}.

By Lemma 5.5(2) we deduce that dQ=dPd_{Q}=d_{P}.

Observe that the sign of f⁡(α)+P⁡(β)f(\alpha)+P(\beta) coincides with that of c⁡(P)c(P), and that of Q⁡(γ)Q(\gamma) coincides with that of c⁡(Q)c(Q); as f⁡(α)+P⁡(β)=Q⁡(γ)f(\alpha)+P(\beta)=Q(\gamma), necessarily c≔c⁡(P)/c⁡(Q)>0c\coloneqq{c(P)}/{c(Q)}>0. Without loss of generality, both c⁡(P)c(P) and c⁡(Q)c(Q) are positive.

Let d=dQ=dPd=d_{Q}=d_{P}. Assume that d>1d>1. By Lemma 5.8 applied twice, once to the polynomials P⁡(x)−xP(x)-x and Q⁡(x)Q(x) and once to the polynomials P⁡(x)+xP(x)+x and Q⁡(x)Q(x), there is n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that

Q⁡(cd​β−n)≤P⁡(β)−β≤f⁡(α)+P⁡(β)≤P⁡(β)+β≤Q⁡(cd​β+n).Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta-n)\leq P(\beta)-\beta\leq f(\alpha)+P(\beta)\leq P(\beta)+\beta\leq Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta+n).

So Q⁡(cd​β−n)≤Q⁡(γ)≤Q⁡(cd​β+n)Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta-n)\leq Q(\gamma)\leq Q(\sqrt[d]{c}\beta+n), and as QQ is increasing on ∗ℕ∖ℕ{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\mathbb{N}, this entails that γ∈[cd​β−n,cd​β+n]\gamma\in[\sqrt[d]{c}\beta-n,\sqrt[d]{c}\beta+n]. So there exists i∈[−n,n]i\in[-n,n] such that γ=⌊cd​β⌋+i\gamma=\lfloor\sqrt[d]{c}\beta\rfloor+i, in particular, ⌊cd​β⌋+i∼β\lfloor\sqrt[d]{c}\beta\rfloor+i\sim\beta, hence ⌊cd​β⌋+i=β\lfloor\sqrt[d]{c}\beta\rfloor+i=\beta. As β\beta is infinite, Fact 2.4(2) gives cd=1\sqrt[d]{c}=1 and i=0i=0, hence γ=β\gamma=\beta. But then f​(α)=(Q−P)​(β)f(\alpha)=(Q-P)(\beta), which forces Q−PQ-P to be constant by Proposition 2.13(6). Since P⁡(0)=0=Q⁡(0)P(0)=0=Q(0), this forces Q=PQ=P, which gives f⁡(α)=0f(\alpha)=0, against the assumptions. Hence d=1d=1.

So we are in the following case:

f⁡(α)+c⁡(P)​β=c⁡(Q)​γ.f(\alpha)+c(P)\beta=c(Q)\gamma.

As c⁡(Q)​γ∼c⁡(Q)​βc(Q)\gamma\sim c(Q)\beta and f⁡(α)≪βf(\alpha)\ll\beta, we conclude by Lemma 5.5(1).∎

In the particular case where f⁡(α)f(\alpha) is a monomial in α\alpha, we can say more:

Corollary 5.10.

Let P⁡(x),Q⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]P(x),Q(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be nonzero polynomials with P⁡(0)=Q⁡(0)=0P(0)=Q(0)=0. Let a,n∈ℕa,n\in\mathbb{N}, and let φ⁡(x,y,z)≔a​xn+P⁡(y)=Q⁡(z)\varphi(x,y,z)\coloneqq ax^{n}+P(y)=Q(z). If φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z then φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is an integer multiple of x+y=zx+y=z or of −x+y=z-x+y=z.

Proof.

Straight from Theorem 5.9, and using the same notations, we get that, by our hypotheses, there is some c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} such that φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is a​xn+c​y=c​zax^{n}+cy=cz. Again, by Theorem 3.8, as φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z there exist (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ∼α\gamma\sim\alpha such that a​αn+c​β=c​γa\alpha^{n}+c\beta=c\gamma.

Fix a prime number pp much larger than a,ca,c (in particular, v⁡(a)=0=v⁡(c)v(a)=0=v(c)), and write α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma in base pp. In the same notation of Section 4, as (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}, by Proposition 2.13(1) and Proposition 2.13(4) we have only two possible cases: v⁡(α)=v⁡(β)v(\alpha)=v(\beta) or v⁡(α)≪v⁡(β)v(\alpha)\ll v(\beta).

Case v⁡(α)=v⁡(β)v(\alpha)=v(\beta).

We divide this case in the two subcases n>1n>1 and n=1n=1.

If n>1n>1, we observe that v⁡(a​αn)=v⁡(a)+n​v​(α)=n​v​(α)v(a\alpha^{n})=v(a)+nv(\alpha)=nv(\alpha). If v⁡(α)≠0v(\alpha)\neq 0 then n​v​(α)>v⁡(α)=v⁡(β)nv(\alpha)>v(\alpha)=v(\beta), so necessarily v⁡(β)=v⁡(γ)v(\beta)=v(\gamma). The same also holds if v⁡(α)=0v(\alpha)=0 because α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma. Let d⁡(t)d(t) be the coefficient of pn​v​(t)p^{nv(t)} in the base pp expansion of tt. The n​v​(γ)nv(\gamma) position in the base pp expansions of both sides of the equation a​αn+c​β=c​γa\alpha^{n}+c\beta=c\gamma gives us that a​smod⁡(α)n+d⁡(c​β)≡d⁡(c​γ)(modp)a\smod(\alpha)^{n}+d(c\beta)\equiv d(c\gamma)\pmod{p}. As dd has finite image we have d⁡(c​β)=d⁡(c​γ)d(c\beta)=d(c\gamma). This implies a​smod⁡(α)n≡0(modp)a\smod(\alpha)^{n}\equiv 0\pmod{p}, which cannot happen since a,smod⁡(α)a,\smod(\alpha) are not divided by pp.

If n=1n=1, then v⁡(a​αn)=v⁡(α)=v⁡(β)v(a\alpha^{n})=v(\alpha)=v(\beta). Using the same notations as above, if v⁡(β)=v⁡(γ)v(\beta)=v(\gamma) then again the equality a​α+c​β=c​γa\alpha+c\beta=c\gamma gives us (a+c)​smod⁡(α)≡c​smod⁡(α)(modp)(a+c)\smod(\alpha)\equiv c\smod(\alpha)\pmod{p}, which is impossible. Hence v⁡(β)<v⁡(γ)v(\beta)<v(\gamma), so it must be a​d+c​d≡0(modp)ad+cd\equiv 0\pmod{p}, namely a≡−c(modp)a\equiv-c\pmod{p}. As pp is much larger than a,ca,c, this tells us that a=−ca=-c.

Case v⁡(α)≪v⁡(β)v(\alpha)\ll v(\beta).

In this case, v⁡(γ)=v⁡(a​αn+c​β)=n​v​(α)v(\gamma)=v(a\alpha^{n}+c\beta)=nv(\alpha) which, as v⁡(γ)∼v⁡(α)v(\gamma)\sim v(\alpha), forces n=1n=1. It follows that that a​smod⁡(α)≡c​smod⁡(γ)(modp)a\smod(\alpha)\equiv c\smod(\gamma)\pmod{p}, which forces a≡c(modp)a\equiv c\pmod{p}. Again, as pp is much larger than a,ca,c, this tells us that a=ca=c.∎

The above result tells us that several well-known PR equations of the form a​xn+P⁡(y)=Q⁡(z)ax^{n}+P(y)=Q(z) are not Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z, for example all equations of the form x−y=Q⁡(z)x-y=Q(z) for deg⁡(Q)>1\deg(Q)>1 and Q⁡(0)=0Q(0)=0 (see [BFM96] for a proof of their partition regularity). Interestingly, such equations can be PR over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, as discussed in the introduction. The reason that our argument breaks over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is simply due to the fact that ℚ\mathbb{Q} contains numbers of arbitrarily small (negative) pp-adic valuation.

As for ±x+y=z\pm x+y=z (over ℕ\mathbb{N}), we have the following.

Proposition 5.11.

Both x+y=zx+y=z and −x+y=z-x+y=z are Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z.

Proof.

As always, by Theorem 3.8 it suffices to find (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ∼α\gamma\sim\alpha such that α+β=γ\alpha+\beta=\gamma or −α+β=γ-\alpha+\beta=\gamma. The x+y=zx+y=z case is well-known: it suffices to take α\alpha such that 𝔲⁡(α)\tp(\alpha) is additively idempotent55 5 The existence of such ultrafilters is also well-known, see e.g. [HS11, Theorem 2.5]. and β\beta such that (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS}, so that by letting γ=α+β\gamma=\alpha+\beta we have that γ∼α\gamma\sim\alpha.

For −x+y=z-x+y=z, pick any infinite η1∼η2∼η3\eta_{1}\sim\eta_{2}\sim\eta_{3} with (η1,η2,η3)(\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\eta_{3}) tensor. Let α=η2−η1,β=η3−η1,γ=η3−η2\alpha=\eta_{2}-\eta_{1},\beta=\eta_{3}-\eta_{1},\gamma=\eta_{3}-\eta_{2}. Then (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} by Proposition 2.17 and α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma as they are all images of equivalent pairs under the same standard function. Clearly, β−α=γ\beta-\alpha=\gamma.∎

Corollary 5.12.

The equations x​y=zxy=z and y=z​xy=zx are Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z.

Proof.

By Proposition 5.11 there is (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} with ±α+β∼α\pm\alpha+\beta\sim\alpha. It then suffices to consider the pair (2α,2β)(2^{\alpha},2^{\beta}). ∎

The equation −x+y=z-x+y=z is the first example we are aware of with the following property.

Remark 5.13.

The formula −x+y=z-x+y=z is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z, but there are no (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} such that −α+β∼α-\alpha+\beta\sim\alpha. Namely, the equation (−u)⊕u=u(-u)\oplus u=u has no solutions in β​ℤ∖ℤ\beta\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

The fact that such (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) cannot exist is well-known, see e.g. [HS11, Corollary 13.19], but here is a quick argument. If (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) are as above, by Puritz’ Theorem we have that v3​(β)∈ℕv_{3}(\beta)\in\mathbb{N} (otherwise smod3⁡(α)=smod3⁡(−α)=3−smod3⁡(α)\smod_{3}(\alpha)=\smod_{3}(-\alpha)=3-\smod_{3}(\alpha), which cannot happen). But then v3​(α)=v3​(β−α)v_{3}(\alpha)=v_{3}(\beta-\alpha), a contradiction because smod3⁡(β)=smod3⁡(α)\smod_{3}(\beta)=\smod_{3}(\alpha), hence v3​(β−α)>v3​(α)v_{3}(\beta-\alpha)>v_{3}(\alpha). ∎

Corollary 5.10 has several more interesting consequences. One regards the non-Ramsey partition regularity of arithmetic progressions, not even in the simplest case of arithmetic progressions of length 33. In particular, there is no “Ramsey version” of van der Waerden’s Theorem.

Proposition 5.14.

The formula

φ⁡(x,y,z)≔“x,y,z form, in some order, an arithmetic progression of length 3”\varphi(x,y,z)\coloneqq\text{``$x,y,z$ form, in some order, an arithmetic progression of length $3$''}

is not Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z.

Proof.

First of all, let us observe that φ⁡(x,y,z)\varphi(x,y,z) is equivalent to

(x+y=2​z)∨(x+z=2​y)∨(y+z=2​x),(x+y=2z)\vee(x+z=2y)\vee(y+z=2x), (2)

whence by Theorem 3.8 to conclude it suffices to prove that there are no α∼β∼γ\alpha\sim\beta\sim\gamma satisfying (2) and such that (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}. But α+β=2​γ\alpha+\beta=2\gamma cannot happen due to Corollary 5.10 applied to P⁡(x)=xP(x)=x and Q⁡(x)=2​xQ(x)=2x. The other two cases are dealt with similarly, by using Corollary 5.10 respectively with P⁡(x)=−2​xP(x)=-2x and Q⁡(x)=−xQ(x)=-x and with P⁡(x)=−xP(x)=-x and Q⁡(x)=xQ(x)=x.∎

Another application of Corollary 5.10 regards ultrafilter equations. It is known that equations of the form a​u⊕b​u=c​uau\oplus bu=cu, where a,b,c∈ℤ∖{0}a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\} and u∈β​ℕu\in\beta\mathbb{N}, can be solved only when a=b=ca=b=c (see [HS11, Theorem 13.18], and see [Mal00] for other results of this kind). By Corollary 5.10 we know that much more is true:

Proposition 5.15.

Let P⁡(x),Q⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]P(x),Q(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] be nonzero polynomials with no constant term. Let a,n∈ℕa,n\in\mathbb{N}. The only equations of the form66 6 Here unu^{n} is the image of the ultrafilter uu under the polynomial function x↦xnx\mapsto x^{n}. This is distinct from u⊙…⊙u⏟n​ times\underbrace{u\odot\ldots\odot u}_{n\text{ times}}. a​un⊕P⁡(u)=Q⁡(u)au^{n}\oplus P(u)=Q(u) that have a solution in β​ℕ\beta\mathbb{N} are the multiples of u⊕u=uu\oplus u=u.

Proof.

Left to right, if the equation a​un⊕P⁡(u)=Q⁡(u)au^{n}\oplus P(u)=Q(u) holds, then for (α,β)⊧u⊗u(\alpha,\beta)\models u\otimes u one has a​αn+P⁡(β)∼Q⁡(α)a\alpha^{n}+P(\beta)\sim Q(\alpha). As TS⊆RW\mathrm{TS}\subseteq\mathrm{RW}, Corollary 5.10 forces deg⁡(P)=deg⁡(Q)=n=1\deg(P)=\deg(Q)=n=1 and a=c⁡(P)=c⁡(Q)a=c(P)=c(Q). By Remark 5.13, a=1a=1. Right to left, any additively idempotent ultrafilter uu solves the given equation. ∎

Another application of Lemma 5.5 is the following generalisation of the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem)..

Proposition 5.16.

Let n,m∈ℤn,m\in\mathbb{Z}, k,r,s∈ℕk,r,s\in\mathbb{N}. Assume that n+m≠0n+m\neq 0. The following are equivalent.

  1. 1.

    There is (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} such that n​α+m​β∼k​αr​βsn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\alpha^{r}\beta^{s}.

  2. 2.

    There is (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} such that n​α+m​β∼k​αr​βsn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\alpha^{r}\beta^{s}.

  3. 3.

    r=s=1r=s=1, one of n,mn,m equals 00, and the other one is positive.

Proof.

1⇒2\ref{point:gensumprodTS}\Rightarrow\ref{point:gensumprodRW} follows from Proposition 2.8.

For 2⇒3\ref{point:gensumprodRW}\Rightarrow\ref{point:gensumprodrsnm}, assume that (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}. Fix a sufficiently large standard prime pp and let v,ℓ,smodv,\ell,\smod be relative to this prime. If n​α+m​β∼k​αr​βsn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\alpha^{r}\beta^{s} then, by applying ℓ\ell to both sides, and possibly replacing ℓ⁡(α)\ell(\alpha) by ℓ⁡(β)\ell(\beta) on the left hand side in the case where m=0m=0, we find ε0,ε1∈ℕ∪{0}\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} such that ℓ⁡(β)+ε0∼r​ℓ​(α)+s​ℓ​(β)+ε1\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon_{0}\sim r\ell(\alpha)+s\ell(\beta)+\varepsilon_{1}. By Lemma 5.5(1) we obtain s=1s=1. If n,m≠0n,m\neq 0, by Lemma 4.3 we obtain v⁡(n​α+m​β)=v⁡(α)v(n\alpha+m\beta)=v(\alpha), hence v⁡(α)∼r​v​(α)+v⁡(β)v(\alpha)\sim rv(\alpha)+v(\beta). The same conclusion still holds if one of n,mn,m equals 00, by an easy calculation. If c=smod⁡(v⁡(α))c=\smod(v(\alpha)) this yields c≡r​c(modp)c\equiv rc\pmod{p} or c≡(r+1)​c(modp)c\equiv(r+1)c\pmod{p} depending on whether v⁡(v⁡(α))=v⁡(v⁡(β))v(v(\alpha))=v(v(\beta)) or not. As rr is positive and much smaller than pp, this implies r=1r=1.

We have now reduced to the case n​α+m​β∼k​α​βn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\alpha\beta. If n,mn,m are both nonzero, an easy modification of the proof of Theorem 4.1 shows that the required (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) cannot be found. As k​α​β>0k\alpha\beta>0, if n=0n=0 then we must have m>0m>0, and symmetrically with the roles of nn and mm interchanged.

For 3⇒1\ref{point:gensumprodrsnm}\Rightarrow\ref{point:gensumprodTS}, we assume that n=0<mn=0<m, the other case being analogous. We need to find (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} such that m​β∼k​α​βm\beta\sim k\alpha\beta. Let α′\alpha^{\prime} be such that 𝔲⁡(α′)\tp(\alpha^{\prime}) is idempotent for ⊙\odot and divisible by kk, and let β′\beta^{\prime} be such that (α′,β′)⊧TS(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime})\models\mathrm{TS}. It then suffices to set α≔m​α′/k\alpha\coloneqq m\alpha^{\prime}/k and β≔m​β′/k\beta\coloneqq m\beta^{\prime}/k. ∎

Remark 5.17.

If we allow r,s∈ℤr,s\in\mathbb{Z}, similar arguments as above yield that, assuming n+m≠0n+m\neq 0, if there is (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} with n​α+m​β∼k​αr​βsn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\alpha^{r}\beta^{s} then (r,s)∈{(1,1),(0,1),(1,0),(−1,1)}(r,s)\in\{(1,1),(0,1),(1,0),(-1,1)\}. The cases (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0) are equivalent and yield n​α+m​β∼k​βn\alpha+m\beta\sim k\beta. By Corollary 5.10 this entails m=k=±nm=k=\pm n. We do not know what happens in the case (r,s)=(−1,1)(r,s)=(-1,1), except for (trivial consequences of) Corollary 5.12.

Let us consider what happens when we relax the Ramsey partition regularity from (x,y),z(x,y),z to (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z.

Proposition 5.18.

Let a,b,c,k1,k2,k3∈ℕa,b,c,k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}\in\mathbb{N}. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    a​xk1+b​yk2=c​zk3ax^{k_{1}}+by^{k_{2}}=cz^{k_{3}} is Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z;

  2. 2.

    k3=1k_{3}=1.

Proof.

1⇒2\ref{point:mortrip1}\Rightarrow\ref{point:mortrip2} Assume, by contrast, that k3>1k_{3}>1. By Theorem 3.8 there exist (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ∈∗ℕ\gamma\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}} such that a​αk1+b​βk2=c​γk3a\alpha^{k_{1}}+b\beta^{k_{2}}=c\gamma^{k_{3}}. Let f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} be defined as follows:

f⁡(y)≔min⁡{z∈ℕ∣c​zk3≥b​yk2}.f(y)\coloneqq\min\{z\in\mathbb{N}\mid cz^{k_{3}}\geq by^{k_{2}}\}.

We claim that f⁡(β)=γf(\beta)=\gamma. In fact, trivially f⁡(β)≤γf(\beta)\leq\gamma. If γ≥f⁡(β)+1\gamma\geq f(\beta)+1 then c​γk3≥c​(f⁡(β)+1)k3c\gamma^{k_{3}}\geq c(f(\beta)+1)^{k_{3}}. Write c​(f⁡(β)+1)k3=c​f​(β)k3+R⁡(β)c(f(\beta)+1)^{k_{3}}=cf(\beta)^{k_{3}}+R(\beta), hence a​αk1+b​βk2≥c​f​(β)k3+R⁡(β)a\alpha^{k_{1}}+b\beta^{k_{2}}\geq cf(\beta)^{k_{3}}+R(\beta). Observe that, as k3≥2k_{3}\geq 2, we have that R⁡(β)R(\beta) is a polynomial in β\beta of degree at least 11. As c​f​(β)k3≥b​βk2cf(\beta)^{k_{3}}\geq b\beta^{k_{2}} by definition of ff, we deduce that a​αk1≥R⁡(β)a\alpha^{k_{1}}\geq R(\beta), and this is in contrast with Proposition 2.13(6).

2⇒1\ref{point:mortrip2}\Rightarrow\ref{point:mortrip1} We just have to take (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} with c|αc\mid\alpha and let γ=(a​αk1+b​βk2)/c\gamma=\left(a\alpha^{k_{1}}+b\beta^{k_{2}}\right)/c.∎

Example 5.19.

Let us show two examples.

  1. 1.

    As recalled before, all equations of the form −x+y=c​zn-x+y=cz^{n} are PR, but the only ones that are Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z are those of the form −x+y=c​z-x+y=cz, among which the only one that is Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z is −x+y=z-x+y=z.

  2. 2.

    Recall (Example 3.2) that the Pythagorean equation x2+y2=z2x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2} is PPR in x,yx,y, equivalently, BPR in x,y|zx,y\mid z. However, by Proposition 5.18 it is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z, hence it is also not Ramsey PR in (x,y),z(x,y),z.77 7 This could have also been deduced directly from Corollary 5.10.

The following general result, close in spirit to the polynomial applications developed so far, shows that many equations involving sums of arbitrary functions are not Ramsey PR.

Proposition 5.20.

Let f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} be such that n↦f⁡(n+1)−f⁡(n)n\mapsto f(n+1)-f(n) is finite-to-one. Then for every g:ℕ→ℕg:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} the equation g⁡(x)+f⁡(y)=f⁡(z)g(x)+f(y)=f(z) is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z.

Proof.

As always, by Theorem 3.8 it suffices to fix (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} and γ∈∗ℕ\gamma\in{}^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}} and prove that g⁡(α)+f⁡(β)≠f⁡(γ)g(\alpha)+f(\beta)\neq f(\gamma). By Proposition 2.13(6) we have f⁡(β+1)−f⁡(β)>g⁡(α)f(\beta+1)-f(\beta)>g(\alpha), hence f⁡(β)<f⁡(β)+g⁡(α)<f⁡(β+1)f(\beta)<f(\beta)+g(\alpha)<f(\beta+1). It follows that f⁡(β)+g⁡(α)f(\beta)+g(\alpha) is not in the image of ff. ∎

Example 5.21.

By Proposition 5.20 the equation x+2y=2zx+2^{y}=2^{z} is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z(x,y)\mid z.

One may ask whether there is a version of Theorem 4.1 involving products and exponentials in place of sums and products. This, and much more, is indeed true, and can be proven by using the following observation.

Proposition 5.22.

Let α,β\alpha,\beta be infinite and f,g:ℕ2→ℕf,g:\mathbb{N}^{2}\to\mathbb{N}. If there are standard functions φ0,φ1,h\varphi_{0},\varphi_{1},h such that

  1. 1.

    φ0​(f⁡(α,β))=φ1​(β)\varphi_{0}(f(\alpha,\beta))=\varphi_{1}(\beta),

  2. 2.

    φ0​(g⁡(α,β))=h⁡(φ1​(β))\varphi_{0}(g(\alpha,\beta))=h(\varphi_{1}(\beta)), and

  3. 3.

    h⁡(φ1​(β))≠φ1​(β)h(\varphi_{1}(\beta))\neq\varphi_{1}(\beta),

then f⁡(α,β)≁g⁡(α,β)f(\alpha,\beta)\nsim g(\alpha,\beta).

Proof.

Otherwise φ0​(f⁡(α,β))∼φ0​(g⁡(α,β))\varphi_{0}(f(\alpha,\beta))\sim\varphi_{0}(g(\alpha,\beta)), hence φ1​(β)∼h⁡(φ1​(β))\varphi_{1}(\beta)\sim h(\varphi_{1}(\beta)), and this would imply h⁡(φ1​(β))=φ1​(β)h(\varphi_{1}(\beta))=\varphi_{1}(\beta). ∎

Note that assumption 3 is true if, e.g., hh has finitely many fixed points.

Let us see some example applications of Proposition 5.22 to some equations involving exponentiation. We begin with the promised “products and exponentials” version of Theorem 4.1.

Example 5.23.

The formula (xy=z)∧(x​y=t)(x^{y}=z)\land(xy=t) is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t.

Proof.

Let f⁡(x,y)=xyf(x,y)=x^{y} and g⁡(x,y)=x​yg(x,y)=xy, and suppose there is (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} with f⁡(α,β)∼g⁡(α,β)f(\alpha,\beta)\sim g(\alpha,\beta). We apply Proposition 5.22 by showing that these two object have different, but very close, exponential level (see e.g. [BM18, Definition 5.2]).

Let ℓ≔ℓ2\ell\coloneqq\ell_{2}, and denote by ℓ(k)\ell^{(k)} the kk-fold composition of ℓ\ell with itself. An easy computation shows that ℓ(3)​(f​(α,β))\ell^{(3)}(f(\alpha,\beta)) is at finite distance from ℓ(2)​(β)\ell^{(2)}(\beta), while ℓ(3)​(g​(α,β))\ell^{(3)}(g(\alpha,\beta)) is at finite distance from ℓ(3)​(β)\ell^{(3)}(\beta). From this observation we can conclude by applying Proposition 5.22 with φ0≔ℓ(3)\varphi_{0}\coloneqq\ell^{(3)}, φ1≔ℓ(2)\varphi_{1}\coloneqq\ell^{(2)} and h⁡(x)≔ℓ⁡(x)+nh(x)\coloneqq\ell(x)+n for a suitable finite n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. ∎

Example 5.24.

The formula (xy=z)∧(yx=t)(x^{y}=z)\land(y^{x}=t) is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t.

Proof.

This is similar to the proof of Example 5.23, with the same φ0\varphi_{0} and φ1\varphi_{1}. ∎

In particular, there is no pair (α,β)⊧TS(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{TS} such that αβ∼βα\alpha^{\beta}\sim\beta^{\alpha}, solving a question from [LB25].

Example 5.25.

The formula (x​2y=z)∧(x+y=t)(x2^{y}=z)\land(x+y=t) is not Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t.

Proof.

If there were (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW} with α​2β∼α+β\alpha 2^{\beta}\sim\alpha+\beta, then (γ,δ)≔(2α,2β)(\gamma,\delta)\coloneqq(2^{\alpha},2^{\beta}) would be in RW\mathrm{RW} and satisfy γδ∼γ​δ\gamma^{\delta}\sim\gamma\delta, against Example 5.23. ∎

Although we deduced the previous example from Example 5.23, it is also a special case of the following.

Example 5.26.

Let f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} be an arbitrary function, m>1m>1 a natural number, and g⁡(x,y):ℕ2→ℕg(x,y):\mathbb{N}^{2}\to\mathbb{N} a function as follows. There is dd such that, for every nn, we have g⁡(n,y)∈𝒪⁡(yd)∩Ω⁡(y1d)g(n,y)\in\mathcal{O}(y^{d})\cap\Omega(y^{\frac{1}{d}}), that is, there are functions h0,h1:ℕ→ℕh_{0},h_{1}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} such that for all n,yn,y we have h0​(n)​y1d≤g⁡(n,y)≤h1​(n)​ydh_{0}(n)y^{\frac{1}{d}}\leq g(n,y)\leq h_{1}(n)y^{d}. If (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}, then f⁡(α)⋅mβ≁g⁡(α,β)f(\alpha)\cdot m^{\beta}\nsim g(\alpha,\beta).

Proof.

This too is similar to the proof of Example 5.23, using φ0=ℓm(2)\varphi_{0}=\ell_{m}^{(2)}, φ1=ℓm\varphi_{1}=\ell_{m}, and hh of the form ℓm​(x)+n\ell_{m}(x)+n. ∎

We conclude this section with a result on polynomial functions. We state it directly in terms of Ramsey’s witnesses.

Proposition 5.27.

Let n,r∈ℤn,r\in\mathbb{Z}, m,s∈ℕm,s\in\mathbb{N}, and (α,β)⊧RW(\alpha,\beta)\models\mathrm{RW}.

  1. 1.

    If n,r,n+m,r+s≠0n,r,n+m,r+s\neq 0 and n​α+m​β∼r​α+s​βn\alpha+m\beta\sim r\alpha+s\beta, then (n,m)=(r,s)(n,m)=(r,s).

  2. 2.

    Let f⁡(x,y)=∑i=0mfi​(x)​yif(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}f_{i}(x)y^{i} and g⁡(x,y)=∑j=0sgj​(x)​yjg(x,y)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}g_{j}(x)y^{j}, where fi,gj:ℕ→ℤf_{i},g_{j}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z} and fm​(α)≠0≠gs​(α)f_{m}(\alpha)\neq 0\neq g_{s}(\alpha). If f⁡(α,β)∼g⁡(α,β)f(\alpha,\beta)\sim g(\alpha,\beta), then m=sm=s.

  3. 3.

    If n,r>0n,r>0 and αn​βm∼αr​βs\alpha^{n}\beta^{m}\sim\alpha^{r}\beta^{s} then (n,m)=(r,s)(n,m)=(r,s).

Proof.
  1. 1.

    By Proposition 2.13(4) we have n​α+m​β≍β≍r​α+s​βn\alpha+m\beta\asymp\beta\asymp r\alpha+s\beta. We apply Lemma 5.5(1) and conclude that m=sm=s. Now let pp be a finite prime much larger than n+m+rn+m+r. Let c≔smodp⁡(α)=smodp⁡(β)c\coloneqq\smod_{p}(\alpha)=\smod_{p}(\beta). If vp​(α)<vp​(β)v_{p}(\alpha)<v_{p}(\beta), then smodp⁡(n​α+m​β)=n​c\smod_{p}(n\alpha+m\beta)=nc and smodp⁡(r​α+m​β)=r​c\smod_{p}(r\alpha+m\beta)=rc, and it follows that n=rn=r. If vp​(α)=vp​(β)v_{p}(\alpha)=v_{p}(\beta) then, by Lemma 4.3,

    (n+m)​c≡smodp⁡(n​α+m​β)≡smodp⁡(r​α+m​β)≡(r+m)​c(modp),(n+m)c\equiv\smod_{p}(n\alpha+m\beta)\equiv\smod_{p}(r\alpha+m\beta)\equiv(r+m)c\pmod{p},

    hence n=rn=r.

  2. 2.

    Observe that ℓ2​(f⁡(α,β))∼ℓ2​(g⁡(α,β))\ell_{2}(f(\alpha,\beta))\sim\ell_{2}(g(\alpha,\beta)). There is ε∈{0,1}\varepsilon\in\{0,1\} such that ℓ2​(f⁡(α,β))=m​ℓ2​(β)+ℓ2​(fm​(α))+ε\ell_{2}(f(\alpha,\beta))=m\ell_{2}(\beta)+\ell_{2}(f_{m}(\alpha))+\varepsilon, hence st⁡(f⁡(α,β)/m​ℓ2​(β))=1\st(f(\alpha,\beta)/m\ell_{2}(\beta))=1. An analogous computation for g⁡(α,β)g(\alpha,\beta) shows that st⁡(g⁡(α,β)/s​ℓ2​(β))=1\st(g(\alpha,\beta)/s\ell_{2}(\beta))=1. It follows from Lemma 5.5(1) applied to f⁡(α,β)f(\alpha,\beta) and g⁡(α,β)g(\alpha,\beta) that st⁡(f⁡(α,β)/g⁡(α,β))=1\st(f(\alpha,\beta)/g(\alpha,\beta))=1, hence m=sm=s.

  3. 3.

    We know from the previous point that m=sm=s. Let π⁡(n)\pi(n) be the smallest prime dividing nn. Observe that π⁡(αa​βb)=π⁡(α)\pi(\alpha^{a}\beta^{b})=\pi(\alpha). Write

    vπ⁡(α)​(αa​βb)=a​vπ⁡(α)​(α)+b​vπ⁡(α)​(β).v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha^{a}\beta^{b})=av_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)+bv_{\pi(\alpha)}(\beta). (3)

    If π⁡(α)<π⁡(β)\pi(\alpha)<\pi(\beta), then the last summand is 00. It follows that n​vπ⁡(α)​(α)∼r​vπ⁡(α)​(α)nv_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)\sim rv_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha), and since vπ⁡(α)​(α)≠0v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)\neq 0 we conclude by Proposition 2.11 that n=rn=r.

    If π⁡(α)=π⁡(β)\pi(\alpha)=\pi(\beta) we have two subcases. If vπ⁡(α)​(α)<vπ⁡(β)​(β)=vπ⁡(α)​(β)v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)<v_{\pi(\beta)}(\beta)=v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\beta) then this pair is in RW\mathrm{RW} by Proposition 2.13(1). We then conclude by applying point 1 above to this pair, using (3). If instead vπ⁡(α)​(α)=vπ⁡(β)​(β)v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)=v_{\pi(\beta)}(\beta), then as vπ⁡(α)​(β)=vπ⁡(β)​(β)v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\beta)=v_{\pi(\beta)}(\beta), by (3) we have (n+m)​vπ⁡(α)​(α)=(r+m)​vπ⁡(α)​(α)(n+m)v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha)=(r+m)v_{\pi(\alpha)}(\alpha), hence again n=rn=r.∎

6 Open problems

The results obtained in this paper open some lines of enquiry that we believe worth investigating further.

Puritz’ Theorem (Fact 2.5) gives a simple characterisation of tensor pairs in terms of standard functions. As for Ramsey pairs, in Proposition 2.13, we have shown that they have several properties that can be expressed in terms of standard functions. Most of our applications actually used some of these properties, so finding a Puritz-like characterisation of Ramsey pairs might be helpful in studying other similar combinatorial problems.

Problem 6.1.

Characterise Ramsey pairs in the style of Puritz’ Theorem.

Problem 6.1 and nonstandard characterisations of related Ramsey properties are the topic of a paper in preparation. Another interesting question regards polynomial equations.

Problem 6.2.

Is it possible to extend Corollary 5.10 from monomials to arbitrary polynomials in xx? To arbitrary multivariate polynomials?

Our proof of Corollary 5.10 uses the fact that it is simple to write the valuation of a monomial in α\alpha in terms of the valuation of α\alpha; the same does not hold for a generic polynomial in α\alpha. An extension of Corollary 5.10 to arbitrary polynomials in xx would give an analogous extension of its corollaries, and in particular of Proposition 5.15.

As observed in Remark 5.17, some variants of the Theorem (Pairwise Sum-Product Theorem). remain open. The most interesting ones seem to be the following. We suspect that solving these should provide enough information to complete the classification.

Problem 6.3.

Which of these formulas are Ramsey PR in (x,y)|z,t(x,y)\mid z,t?

  1. 1.

    (−x+y=z)∧(x​y=t)(-x+y=z)\land(xy=t).

  2. 2.

    (−x+y=z)∧(y=t​x)(-x+y=z)\land(y=tx).

  3. 3.

    (x+y=z)∧(y=t​x)(x+y=z)\land(y=tx).

Our final question essentially asks to deal with the “never considered” cases of Tables 1, 2 and 3 from Section 4.

Problem 6.4.

In which partitions of the variables is the formula (x≠y)∧(x+y=z)∧(x⋅y=t)\left(x\neq y\right)\wedge\left(x+y=z\right)\wedge\left(x\cdot y=t\right) BPR? In which ones is it Ramsey PR?
